=== Domain 3: Services and Networking ===


--- Overview of Container Orchestration - New ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video at an overview, we are going to discuss about the basics of container orchestration.
Now again this video is going to be very important.
Specifically before you learn any orchestration tools like Kubernetes, swarm, ECS, etc. this video
will act as a base that will make things easier for learning any orchestration tool.
So with this, let's get started.
Now before we discuss about container orchestration, it is important for us to take a step back to
see what users and organization used to do before these tools became much more mature, to be ready
to serve production level traffic.
Now, during the initial times, users relied on manual container management tool to handle various
tasks like launching containers, managing containers, and so on.
For example, let's say that you have a server and you have a user, and user wants to launch some containers
for his application or his website.
So what he will do first, he will manually login to the server, and then he will run certain commands
like docker run to create the appropriate containers required for the application to run.
Now this is good from a smaller scale environment.
Generally, during earlier times, organizations were much more mature where they would have some kind
of an automation script, maybe through Python, shell scripts, etc. that used to take care of common
tasks like deployment, scaling, networking, monitoring, etc..
Now, irrespective of both the approaches that we are discussing here, when the environment becomes
larger, specifically in production environment, both the approaches are not really sufficient to handle
things at scale.
So let's take few common examples that almost all of the organizations use to face.
And then we'll see on how container orchestration comes into picture.
So first challenge here is related to manual scaling.
So let's say that you have a server one where there are two containers that are running now suddenly
as part of your promotion or maybe some kind of advertisement, you are receiving very high traffic
on your website.
And the issue is that there is only one container running for app, one container running for nginx.
So in the situation where there is an unexpected high amount of traffic that is coming to your website,
you want some form of scaling to happen.
Now you also have a second server that is available.
However, this scaling will not really happen automatically.
So now what will happen is the user or the developer.
He will have to manually create the container on the second server as well.
And then whatever traffic that comes to your website, it needs to be load balanced between the containers
in the server one and server number two.
So all of this is a manual process and it takes a lot of time.
Now let's explore one more very common challenge that organizations used to face specifically related
to fault tolerance.
So let's say that you have some containers that are running in the server one.
Now if a container has failed, it can be due to a wide variety of reasons.
It can be a crash, it can be due to resource exhaustion, etc. the container generally would not automatically
restart without manual intervention in most of the cases.
Now at this stage we are just taking an example where app container has failed.
However, what happens if the entire server one has failed?
How would you automate things in such cases?
So when you have a manual based approach, if the server one fails what you might do in the server two
again you will launch the app container.
You will launch the nginx container, redirect the traffic to the server two and so on.
So all of this is a manual process and it makes things difficult for production level environments.
So these are just two common challenges that a wide variety of other challenges also that organizations
were facing.
And in order to overcome all of these, you have a new technology of container orchestration that came
into picture.
Now at a very high level overview of container orchestration automates the deployment, management,
scaling and networking of the containers.
So now what will happen is you have a container orchestration tool which is responsible for all of this
task.
Now user let's say a user wants to launch certain containers in a fleet of servers.
So he will not manually log in to each of the server, manually run the docker run command to create
a container, and so on.
So that is the older approach.
So now in the newer approach where container orchestration is used, user will communicate directly
to the container orchestration tool.
And container orchestration tool will in turn take care of the responsibility of launching the containers
in the appropriate server, making sure that this containers are always running.
If the containers are not running, let's say if a server one has crashed, then container orchestration
tool has that logic to migrate that container or relaunch the container in another server to ensure
that containers are always running.
So most of the common tasks related to deployment scaling, networking, everything.
Container orchestration tool takes care of it.
So let's look into how container Orchestration tool allows us to solve some of the important challenges
that organizations used to face.
So let's say that you have in total of three servers that are running as part of the fleet.
As of now, the traffic is less.
So you have 25% of traffic, and the container orchestration tool has launched one container in server
number one.
Note that many of the mature container orchestration tool can automatically scale the containers up
or down, based on the defined policies and the real time traffic.
This is the important part to understand.
So let's say as of now the traffic is less.
You only have one container, but at a later stage you have increased the amount of traffic.
So you have 75% of traffic that is coming.
So this single container might not be able to handle all of the requests.
So now what container orchestration will do.
It will go ahead and launch multiple set of containers in multiple servers.
and also the traffic will be routed equally among all of the servers.
And this is a great benefit for organizations.
Along with that, we were discussing about the challenge related to fault tolerance.
Now when container orchestration is introduced, it can automatically look into the health check of
the containers that are running.
And let's say that the server one has crashed due to some reason.
Then container orchestration will go ahead and it has the appropriate logic to create one more set of
containers in another server and redirect all of the traffic to server number two so that the website
is always running.
So all of this important logic, you don't really have to create the manual scripts related to it.
The container orchestration tool automatically takes care of it.
And this is of great benefit and it saves huge amount of time.
Great.
So now that we understand the basic of it at an overview, let's have a quick demo to understand on
how things really work.
Now for today's demo video I have three servers that are created.
One is where you have a container orchestration tool that is available, and you have two more servers
which are going to be the worker node where the actual containers can run.
So let's go ahead and quickly connect to this server post, which will be discussing things in more
detail.
Great.
So currently I am connected to all of the three servers.
Now as we are discussing, when you have a container orchestration tool that comes into picture, user
will not really log in to each of the server.
Manually launch the container, route the traffic accordingly.
What user will do?
He will instruct the container orchestration tool that say I need five containers of nginx and container
orchestration tool has the appropriate logic to launch the five containers and ensure that they are
always running.
So let's take an example where I instruct that in total I need five containers of nginx that should
be running now.
Again, we are not interested in the command at this stage.
We are more interested to see on how things work at a high level.
Overview.

to take whatever instruction that you have provided, and it will act on it to ensure that in total,
five containers will be created and will always be running.
Now, as we are discussing that there are multiple worker servers that are running.
In fact, the containers can also run on the main manager node in case if you have configured it.
So let's look into it.

Now as we were discussing That container orchestration tool also ensures that whatever instruction that
you have provided, it gets fulfilled all of the time.
For example, we have told the container orchestration that I need a total of five containers of nginx
that would be running now, let's say due to some reason the worker zero two server has crashed.
All right, so let me do one thing.

that these two containers that were running in the worker zero two, which is no longer present, these
two containers are created in the remaining servers, whatever are running.

that got created in the worker zero one.
Why?
Because worker zero two is no longer responding.
All right.
So this is one very simple example related to what container orchestration tool allows us to do.
Now one thing to note is that container orchestration tool is a lot more.
Now just for this video we had taken two examples related to manual scaling and fault tolerance.
However, there are a lot of important features that the container Orchestration tool provides from
the perspective of production environment, which is very helpful.
For example, load balancing and traffic routing monitoring of container health.
Along with that, one point to note is that there are many container orchestration tools that are available
in the industry, and based on the requirement, you can use one among them.
For example, Docker Swarm has been one of the very popular container orchestration tool that was initially
used.
Nowadays in the industry, if you speak, Kubernetes is extremely popular and in fact most of the organization
seems to be using Kubernetes because of the wide range of extensive features that it provides.
When we discuss about AWS, you also have EKS.
Again, it is a container orchestration that is available.
For example, let's also explore.
So when it comes to AWS you have the Elastic Container Service.
If you see it is a fully managed container orchestration service.
Now at this stage we have understood at a high level overview on what container orchestration allows
you to do.
So I hope this makes better sense now.
Then the second one is the Docker swarm.
Again, this is something that is used not so extensively nowadays, but it was very popular earlier
and the most popular in the industry nowadays is Kubernetes.
Again, a great container orchestration with extensive set of features.
And it really makes things much more easier.
And you can literally run things at an enterprise grade scale without facing scalability and other issues.
Great.
Now, before we conclude, one pointer that I wanted to share is that irrespective of the container
orchestration tool that you choose at a high level overview.
As we were discussing, the main task of container orchestration remains to be the same.
However, depending upon the tool that you choose, the features that are available will change drastically.
For example, when we compare Docker Swarm with Kubernetes, there is a huge difference in terms of
features.
Docker swarm does not have too many features.
However, when it comes to Kubernetes, it has extensive set of features compared to any other container
orchestration tool that is available in the industry.
And this is the reason why, again, Kubernetes is so popular and why so many organizations are using
it quite extensively.
All right.

For example, when we discuss about Docker Swarm it is very easy to set up.

with the Docker Swarm, but again, Kubernetes.

Itself.

Container orchestration tool that you might choose will be different.
For example you need a.
Very simple setup for container orchestration because you do not really have a manpower or expertise.
So in such cases, we have seen that organizations use very simple setup based on Docker Swarm or maybe
even EKS.
But in a large scale organization, in enterprises where you have a manpower, you have the required
capabilities, and you need some tool to manage thousands and tens of thousands of containers at scale.
In such cases, Kubernetes is something that proves to be very useful.

=== Domain 4: Security ===


--- Introduction to Kubernetes - New ---

Hi everyone, and welcome to the introductory video to Kubernetes.
Now, before we proceed further, one thing that I wanted to share is that personally, I have used
a wide range of container orchestration tools that are available in the industry.
It can be Docker Swarm, it can be Amazon, EKS and various others that are available.
But by far one of the best ones that is available in the industry is Kubernetes.
So we are going to discuss about Kubernetes in great detail step by step.
So with this base set let's go ahead and understand the basics of Kubernetes.
Now at a high level overview.
One point to note is that Kubernetes is an open source container orchestration engine developed by Google.
So although it was originally designed by Google, but now it is maintained by CNCF, which is the cloud
native computing Foundation.
Now with this base set, let's go ahead and look into the architecture of Kubernetes at an overview.
There are two important components of the Kubernetes cluster.
First, very important one is the control plane.
And the second one is the worker nodes.
Now control plane is the actual Kubernetes cluster.
So all of the main components that are part of Kubernetes, they are referred to as the control plane.
And the worker nodes that you see on the right.
These are the actual servers where the container applications run.
All right.
So let's also look into the workflow at a high level overview.
So discussing about the workflow the user communicates to the control plane and provides the necessary
instruction to run the containerized applications.
For example you have a user user will have some requirements.
For example user might want to run two containers of nginx.
Or user might want to run an application container, but not on the smaller server on the largest server
that is available here.
So all of these requirements, the user will submit it to the control plane, which is the main Kubernetes
master node.
Control plane will interpret the requirement, and it will go ahead and launch the appropriate container
in the nodes that are available as part of the overall cluster.
All right.
So this is a very basic high level workflow.
Now before we proceed further, let me also quickly show you on how exactly it looks like so that things
are much more clear.

back from Kubernetes.

--- Basics of Pods ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about a very important topic in Kubernetes which is pods.
Now pods are one of the Kubernetes objects that you will be using quite extensively in real world environment
and also in terms of exams.
So let's go ahead and understand the basics of Kubernetes Pods post, which will be discussing things
in more detail.
Now in order to understand about Kubernetes Pod, first let's take a simple analogy related to Docker.
So what does this state?
It states that.
Let's assume that you have recently installed Docker in your system.
Now what is the first thing that you might do.
So you have Docker available.
What is the first thing that you might do.
You might go ahead and try to create a container to see on how exactly things work.
In a very similar terms, if you have Kubernetes cluster that is recently configured, what is the first
thing that you might do?
You might go ahead and try to create a pod.
Now, the overall approach, both at a Docker as well as the Kubernetes way is quite similar.
However, the naming convention that you will see is a little different.
In Docker we call it as container.
In Kubernetes we call it as pod.
Both are very similar.
So let's go ahead and understand the difference between both of them, so that it makes things much
more clear now at a high level.
Overview.
The primary difference between a Docker container and a Kubernetes pod is that a pod can contain one
or more Docker containers.
This is very important part to remember.
And these containers that are part of the pod, they share the same network namespace as well as storage
volumes.
For example, you have a pod.
Now in this pod, it can happen that there are multiple set of containers that are running.
And these containers, since they share the same network, they can intercommunicate between each other
using local host.
However, at an overview, just note that pod is nothing but a container.
It can be a single container based pod.
It can be a multi container based pod.
So if your concept related to Docker container is clear, then Pod is something very, very similar.
Now as part of this video, we are going to go ahead and compare as well as implement Docker set of
commands versus Kubernetes set of commands.
For example, let's say you want to create a new container in Docker.
What you will do you will run for example docker run nginx.
In Kubernetes the equivalent command would be kubectl run nginx followed by image of nginx.
Now if you see the commands are also quite similar.
So if you know the basics of Docker, it will be easier for you to quickly understand the Kubernetes
set of commands as well.
Related to pods.
All right.
So let's do one thing.
Let's go ahead and quickly try this out so that we understand things in a better way.
Now as part of today's practical I have a server where I have Docker that is installed.
You do not really need this server.
I am using this so that we can have a comparative analysis.
All you need is a Kubernetes cluster clustered to create the equivalent command with kubectl.
So the first command as we are looking in Docker is you go ahead and create a container.
So even in the earlier slide, we saw that one of the first things that you will do is you might create
a container here.
So in a Docker based server I'll go ahead and I'll create a container.
Let's run a command say docker run nginx.
What it will do.
It will go ahead and create a container for us in a similar way as we know in Kubernetes we refer to
it as pod.
So we'll say kubectl run nginx followed by the image that you want the pod to use, in this case nginx.
I'll press enter and you see a pod of nginx is created.
Now the second command here is docker PS.
What does this do.
It allows you to list the running containers.
The equivalent command would be kubectl get pods.
So for example we have this nginx container that is running.
So if I run say docker PS you see we have this nginx container that is running.
So it basically shows you a list of running containers.
Now equivalent command in Kubernetes is kubectl get pods.
And you see it shows you that we have one pod that is running.
The third command here is docker logs followed by the container.
What it does it allows us to see the logs associated with it.
So for example if I say docker logs followed by the container id, you see this is the logs that we
are seeing in a similar way when it comes to Kubernetes.
When you say kubectl logs followed by the name of pod, in this case it is nginx.
And you see you are getting a similar output to that of docker.
The next important command is docker inspect followed by container.
It basically allows you to get detailed information about a container.
So for example I say docker inspect followed by the container ID will just clear the screen and you
see it shows you detail information related to this.
So if I go a bit up it shows details related to IP addresses, the image based on which the container
is running and so on.
So all of this information has been provided to you.
Now when we discuss about the Kubernetes pod you can say kubectl describe pod nginx.
And similarly here also you get detailed information related to it.
For example here you see that this is the IP address, the node in which the pod is running and so on.
All right.
The next important command is to execute a interactive shell.
So basically let's say that you have this Docker container that is running.
Now you want to login Logging inside this Docker container.
Generally, when we discuss about Docker, we run this command followed by the container id and you
can just specify bash.
Considering that the container image has bash, this will work.
And now you see you are logged in inside the Docker container.
So this is inside Docker container.
Similarly when we discuss about Kubernetes pod you can run kubectl exec followed by the name of pod
followed by bash.
And now you see I got logged in inside the nginx container.
Let's do a ctrl d to come out of it at both the places.
And the last command that we are going to explore is to remove a container or to remove a pod.
Now in Docker the overall command is docker rm, which is docker remove followed by container.
In Kubernetes it is kubectl delete pod followed by the name.
Now in docker I'll just do a control c and we'll just do a docker rm followed by the name of the container
or the container id, and that's about it.
Our container is removed.
So if you do a docker PS it is no longer present docker PS hyphen a, which also shows you stopped containers.
It is no longer present.
Now in Kubernetes you can just do a kubectl delete pod followed by the name of pod which is nginx and
this will delete the pod.
Now if you just do a kubectl get pods, you see no pods are currently running.
Great.
So I hope with this comparison table and the associated practical both at a Docker and Kubernetes level,
I hope this has made you a little comfortable with the kubectl set of commands specifically related

Now, before we conclude few important pointers that you have to keep a note specifically related to
Kubernetes pod.
First one is that a pod always runs on a node.
As we have learned, pod is nothing but a container.
So container needs a specific node to run.

--- Generating Manifest File through CLI Command ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about an interesting topic on how we can generate a manifest
file through CLI command.
Now at this stage we know two important things.
First is that the CLI commands are quite easy to run, so you can go ahead and quickly create a new
pod using the kubectl command.
This is one learning.
Second important learning is that manifest files are also used to create the object in Kubernetes.
And this is the preferred way in production environments.
Why?
Because it provides a wide set of benefits like version control, team collaboration, etc..
So based on this important learning, we know that creating manifest file is something that is little
time consuming and you do not really want to do it for all of the object that you might create.
So you need to find an easier way in which the manifest files are automatically generated for you.
For example, you have a kubectl command to create a object like pod, and this command should automatically
generate the appropriate manifest file for you so that you can deploy your object using the manifest
file, and then you can add it as part of the version control.
So this is a much more better approach.
So in today's video we are going to look exactly into how we can use kubectl to generate a manifest
file.
Now before we do that there are two important flags that you can add as part of the kubectl command
that we need to understand.
First important one is dry run is equal to client.
So when you add this as part of your kubectl command it validates a Kubernetes resource definition without
actually applying it to the cluster.
So for example in the output here you see you have pod nginx created.
And in the bracket you have dry run.
So the actual object is not really created in Kubernetes but the validation has been completed.
In fact let's also look into it now from my CLI.
When I do kubectl get pods.

Here you are.

Now the first important part is related to how you can define command and arguments as part of a manifest
file.
When we discuss about that, there are two primary ways that you will generally see in documentation,
as well as many of the tutorials.
The first one is using an array, so it is something similar to a square brackets where you can go ahead
and add command and arguments.
This is something that we have been using.
However, you also have a different approach of multi-line YAML list for each new item.
So if you look into the first approach over here, so what you can do in the command, you have the
square brackets here and in the square brackets you can go ahead and add whatever command that you want
the container to run.
So this is easy to understand.
The second approach of multi-line YAML list is also something that you might see.
So in this, what you do in the command, you don't add a square brackets.
Here you have a hyphen followed by exact command that you want to run.
Bin sh is here, then C is here.

Now the expose instruction, it informs Docker that a container listens on a specified network port
at a runtime.
So let's say that you have a Docker image and the service or the application within that Docker image
is listening on port number 5000.
So how will a individual who is running the Docker container know that a service is listening on Port
5000 because the service can listen on 8000, 9000 or any ephemeral port.
So the expose instruction precisely informs on that aspect.
Now, as we are discussing, the primary aim of expose instruction is not actually to publish the port,
but to inform on which port a specific application or a specific service is running.
So if you want to actually publish a port at a Docker level, then you will have to use the hyphen P
option.
So the third point, as it states that this expose instruction, it functions as type of a documentation
between the person who builds the image and the person who runs the container about which port are intended
to be published.

--- Overview of ReplicaSets - NEW ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about replica set.
So let us go ahead and first understand the challenge that organizations use to face post, which will
be discussing on how replica set can solve them.
So a simple use case which states that there is a requirement to run three pods based on nginx image
all the time.
Now if you see this requirement, what you will do, you will go ahead and you will have certain set
of kubectl run commands, maybe directly.
Or you might create a manifest file for each pod that you want to create.
And then you will use the set of commands to go ahead and create three set of pods based on the Kubernetes
cluster.
Now, when we compare it with the requirement, the first part of the requirement has been completed
which states run three pods based on the nginx image.
But the second part, which is all the time, is not ensured when you go through this manual approach.
For example, when we discuss about one of the primary issues here, in case if a pod fails now, it
can happen that the pod has failed directly, or the node based on which the pod has been running has
crashed.
In such cases, the Kubernetes will not automatically recreate the pod.
So, for example, let's say the nginx pod one has stopped working.
Nginx pod two has stopped working.
So in such case, Kubernetes will not automatically recreate the pod.
Now it can happen that the entire worker node, which hosts all of the three pods, has stopped working
altogether.
Again, in such case, Kubernetes will not recreate those pods.
So whenever you have situations where there are node failures, etc., then you will have to manually
detect those failures and recreate the pod in the appropriate working node.
This is the major issue that you will face.
The second issue that you will typically face specifically in the longer term is related to scalability.
So today the requirement is related to three pods.
But what happens is after one week, the requirement is to run 20 pods based on the nginx image.
Are you going to go ahead and copy paste the command of kubectl run 20 times.
Or are you going to go ahead and have multiple set of manifest file and do a kubectl apply for each
of the manifest file?
The answer is yes, you can do that, but it is time consuming.
So in order to implement a requirement that we discuss as part of today's video and overcoming the challenges
as well, you have a specific resource of replica set.
Now, the main aim of the replica set is to maintain a stable set of pods that would be running at a
given amount of time.
For example, same requirement where you want to go ahead and run three pods of nginx image all of the
time.
Now, instead of directly going ahead and creating Pod manually, you inform this requirement to the
replica set.
You tell replica set that I need three pods of nginx image and replica set will take care of creation
and maintenance of the pod.
So if tomorrow if pod one has crashed and it is not running, replica set will go ahead and create one
more port to ensure that three ports run all of the time.
This is a very big advantage of this specific object.
So with this base set, let's go ahead and look into it from a demo perspective.
And we'll have a separate video associated with the practicals.
Now for today's video I already have a replica set that is created.
So if I do kubectl get replica set, you see we have a replica set called as Web server hyphen replica
set and desired is basically a way of informing replica set that I need a total of three pods running
all of the time.
The current is basically how many pods are running currently as part of the environment.
It is three, so ideally in replica set the desired and current should match.
Now if I do kubectl get pods, you see I have three pods that are running based on this specific replica
set.
Now as we were discussing that it is now, the replica sets responsibility to ensure that three pods
run all of the time if one of the pod crashes or the node on which the pod is running crashes, then
replica set has the appropriate logic to recreate the pod in different node.
So just for simplicity, let's go ahead and manually delete one of the pods.
All right I'll delete this specific pod.
All right.
Now when you do kubectl get pods again immediately you see a new pod got recreated by the replica set.
So you see the age of the pod is just four seconds.
It is so fast.
All right.
So I hope with this you understood on how replica set can take care of this manual.
Part of monitoring and recovering from pod failures.
The second part that we were discussing is related to manual scaling of pods.
So for example, let's say currently three pods are enough, but tomorrow I need ten pods.
Now, when it comes to replica set, we don't really have to manually create the pods.
We can inform the replica set now.
Again, this command will be discussing at a later stage so we can manually inform the replica set that
I need a total of, say, ten parts, and you just define which replica set you are targeting.
In our case, it is web server replica set.
All right.
Now again, we will be discussing this at a later stage in the practical video.
But at this stage you see it stays.
Web server replica set has scaled.
Now when we look into the replica set over here, you see the desired is ten, the current is ten.
Now when you do kubectl get pods over here, you have ten pods running based on the appropriate image.
Now tomorrow let's say the promotion has completed and you no longer require all of the ten pods.
You want to go back to three pods.
So again you can simply specify that I need three pods that are running and that's about it.
When you do kubectl get pods, you see the seven extra pods have been removed and the three older pods
are currently running.
All right.
So I hope with this at a high level overview, you understood the importance of replica set in Kubernetes.

--- Challenges with ReplicaSets ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video, we are going to discuss about some of the important challenges specifically related
to replica set that you should be aware of.
Now, before we explore some of the challenges, one important part that we need to be aware of is that
replica sets are primarily designed to run a specific set of pods.
It can be three pod, five pod, etc. however, they are not designed to handle regular updates or changes
to their configuration.
This is a very important part to note, and this is the reason why some of the important challenges
that you will face in replica set based configuration is related to updates or changes as part of their
configuration.
So let's take a simple example that will allow us to understand things in more detail.
So let's take a scenario where you have a user.
User has informed replica set that a total of three pods based on nginx image needs to run all the time,
and replica set in turn has created three nginx spot.
This is great.
Now the problem that happens is that maybe at a later stage you have decided that you need a different
version of nginx, the higher version of nginx that was recently released, or maybe a different image
altogether.
In such cases, generally, when you update the pod template as part of the replica set, the existing
pods are not updated.
So, for example, let's say that you change the image as part of the pod template from Nginx to Apache.
A replica set is not going to update the existing pod, and this can create a lot of issues.
Let's go ahead and quickly look into it.
So for today's video I have a very simple manifest file based on replica set.
And this is based on nginx image.
I'll also be adding the code in the GitHub page.
Now when you go ahead and do a kubectl apply on the file, we have the replica set that is created.
Now when you do a kubectl get replica set You see, total desired is three.
The current is three.
This is good.
And when you do a kubectl get pods, you have three pods based on the replica set that is running.
Now let's say that tomorrow a newer version of application got released.
Now again, just for simplicity, we have used nginx, but in a production environment you will have
application version, right?
So currently let's assume that you have version one of the app running.
So something like this.
But maybe after 10 or 15 days there is new version two of app that is released.
So what you'll typically do for the replica set, you will update the image over here with the latest
version.
Now just for simplicity, I'll change it to httpd, which is the Apache web server.
Now, generally when you make the change to the pod spec and when you go ahead and apply that same change
over here.
The apply is completed.
So now what?
You will assume that these web servers would be replaced by the newer version of the application.
In our case, it would be replaced by the Apache web server.
However, when you do a kubectl get pods, you see no new pods are created.
The older pods are still running over here.
Now when you do a kubectl describe replica set web server replica set.
So at this stage you see in the image it is showing us as httpd latest.
So from here we can determine that replica set configuration by itself was updated successfully.
However, the pods as part of the replica set are not updated here.
So just to verify you can just do a kubectl get pods, you will see that you have the older pods that
are running and you can also do a cube CTL describe pod.
Just take one pod name over here you can look into the image.
The image of the pod is still nginx.
All right.
So I hope with this you understood this important challenge one.
And this is the reason why, in the first slide a pointer was added which states that the main aim of
replica set is to maintain certain state of running pods.
So in this case the replicas is three.
So three pods will always be running, but it is not designed to handle regular updates or changes to
the configuration, primarily the pod spec.
Now at this stage.
If you go ahead and delete the pod, let me quickly show you this is interesting and important to know.
So let's say that when you delete the pod.
So now what will happen is in the replica set configuration we have added images httpd.
So whatever newer pods that gets created as part of replica set, those newer pods will be based on
the newer configuration.
All right.
So this issue related to the updates not been applicable is only related to the existing pod, not the
newer pod.
So if I delete the pod over here now if you do a kubectl get pods, you will see that one more pod has
been started by the replica set.
So this newer pod will use the latest configuration whatever is been defined.
So now if you do a cube CTL describe pod you can copy the pod name here.
And if you will see this pod is based on the httpd latest image.
All right.
So this is one important part to remember.
Again in a production environment this is not the desired state that you always like.
Because if you have one newer version of application and two pods based on older version of application,
then users might face lot of issues which you do not really want.
So in such cases you can just say kubectl scale replica set Asset web server, replica set and replicas
you can set to zero.
You can do kubectl get pods.
There are no pods.
And now you can go ahead and set the replica sets again to three.
And when you do a kubectl get pods now all of the pods that would be created would be based on the latest
image.
However, in this approach of zero and three, you see that at a stage there are no pods that are running,
so you do not really want to do it in production environment because your website will stop running.
And when there are thousands of users, this is a big no no.
Alright, so again this is good for our knowledge and testing environment, but not for the production
environment.
The second important challenge that you need to know is that there is no rollback mechanism that is
inbuilt as part of replica set.
For example, let's say that you have a specific state of replica set configuration.
It can be image of a replica set and you make some changes and you have the state number two.
Now you realize that there are some issues related to state number two, and you would like to revert
it to the previous state.
So in order for this rollback to happen, there is no direct inbuilt feature that is part of replica
set that supports this.
Now generally in production environments there are thousands of deployments that you will see regularly
happening.
Now among those thousands of deployments, it can happen.
20 or 30 deployments are not really working.
So you want to quickly roll back.
So this is one of the features that is not part of replica set.
And the third challenge that you will generally see is related to the label collision.
This also is quite important.
So let's say that you have created a replica set.
And in the selector of that replica set you have defined app is equal to test hyphen app.
So now what will happen is all of the pod which has this specific label will be added and will be managed
by the replica set.
Now, in case if there is some external part that you have created already earlier.
So let's say replica set you created today, but this specific part is running since past three months.
Now this part also has the same label that is added as part of the selector.
Now what will happen is replica set will automatically start to manage this specific part, and it can
also delete the part when you specifically scale down the operation.
So this again can have unintended consequences.
So you have to be quite careful.
So let us take an example.

--- Overview - Multiple Worker Nodes Based Cluster ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about multiple worker nodes that can be added as part of
the Kubernetes cluster and its associated benefits.
Now, one point that needs to be noted specifically, if you have a Kubernetes cluster with a single
worker node environment, is that the worker node also has a certain set of limitations.
For example, let's say that this node one has one GB of Ram and one CPU.
So can it run one pod?
Yes it can.
Can it run 100 pods?
It might not.
Why?
Because this specific worker node does not have enough resources to run 100 pods.
Or it can also happen.
That one pod that you might want to run over here requires huge amount of memory and CPU, and this
node might not be able to handle it.
So this is the reason why generally in a production level Kubernetes cluster, you will not see just
one worker node.
There can be multiple sets.
There can be hundreds.
There can even be thousands.
All right.
So at a high level overview, one point that we need to note is that adding a worker node to your overall
Kubernetes cluster will distribute the workload across the worker node.
So, for example, let's say that you are scheduling 100 pods.
So will all the 100 pods be scheduled in the node one?
Answer is no.
They will be distributed across node one.
Node two.
Node three.
And in this way, since the overall workload is distributed, maximum number of pods will be able to
run as part of the Kubernetes cluster.
And as part of Kubernetes, it is not necessary that you have started a Kubernetes cluster with one
node.
Now you cannot add node two whenever you require.
You can go ahead and easily add multiple set of worker nodes based on the requirement.
Now tomorrow you only have 1 or 2 pods that would be running.
So do you really need three nodes?
Answer is not necessarily.
You might even choose to use two node based cluster to save costs.
So depending upon the requirement, you can increase and decrease the overall worker node accordingly.
Now I also wanted to share a few more benefits associated with having a Having a multiple worker nodes
in a Kubernetes cluster.
One primary benefit is related to fault tolerance.
So let's assume that you only have one worker node.
And if that one worker node fails, then whatever application pod that was running on that node will
become unavailable.
And this is something that you do not really want.
So in case if you have multiple worker nodes and a worker node went down, then you can or even Kubernetes
can reschedule that pod from that failed worker node to the other running worker node so that your application
becomes running all of the time.
Now, it is also important for us to know on how you can see how many nodes are part of your Kubernetes
cluster.
And the command is very simple.
It is kubectl get nodes.
So if you look into the first screenshot you have one worker node.
And it also shows you what is the Kubernetes version that is being used as part of this.
And in the second screenshot over here, you see there are three worker nodes that are available.
Now generally when you are learning Kubernetes then one worker node is quite decent enough.
However, when you implement Kubernetes for the production environment, then you should ideally have
multiple set of worker nodes.
Now again, it will increase the cost, but the production environment can be much more safer in such
cases.
So let's go ahead and also look into it from a demo perspective.
So as we were discussing that you can use the kubectl get nodes command to go ahead and check how many
worker nodes that are available.

present when you create a Kubernetes cluster.
You can go ahead and increase or decrease the number of worker nodes whenever you require.
So just for example, let's explore the managed Kubernetes cluster that we have in DigitalOcean.

three.
If I open this, you see there are in total of three worker nodes.
And you can increase it as well based on the requirement.
Now one very important point that we need to note is that it is not necessary that all worker nodes

--- Overview of Node Selector ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.

Now one point that you should note is that generally in a production environment where Kubernetes cluster
is deployed, you will see that there are multiple set of worker nodes.

For example, here you can assume that node one is having two GB of Ram.
Node two is having eight GB of Ram.
Node three is having one GB of Ram.
So the Kubernetes supports different worker node with different hardware specifications.
This is one point to note.
Second important point to note is that whenever you schedule a pod on a specific worker node, you should
also know what are the requirements that pod needs.
Some pod might run application that would require more amount of CPU and memory, while some other pod
will require a very basic bare minimum compute resources to run.
So depending upon what exactly the applications require in terms of CPU and CPU and memory, you can
go ahead and select the appropriate node for that specific port to run.
And one of the approaches that you can use to achieve this is using node selector.
So at a high level overview, node selector allows us to control the placement of pod into a specific
node of a cluster.
So let's take a simple requirement here which states that app a pod requires high memory and CPU.
Run it in a big node.
Now within these three worker nodes that you see, which is the bigger node, the bigger node is node
two.

well.

app a pod to node number three, where it will not really work well.
So this is the reason why node selector is quite useful.

--- Overview of Node Affinity ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to go ahead and discuss about node affinity.
Now one prerequisite for this video is that you need to know about the basics of node selector.
We have already discussed about node selector in the previous videos, so make sure that your concept
is better understood related to that topic before proceeding with node affinity.
Now, one point that we need to note is that in a node selector based approach, it uses a method of
strict equality.
How?
By using the selector to match the appropriate label in the worker node.
For example, in this worker node you have a label of size equals to medium.
So if you want a pod to run on this worker node in the node selector of that pod, you have to ensure
that you add size equal to medium.
And then only the pod will be scheduled here.
Now this is a very basic way of scheduling a pod to a specific node.
However, generally in production environments, when you have hundreds to thousands of worker nodes,
this basic approach of node selector might not always suit such environments.
So in order to have much more flexible option, you have one more feature of node affinity that is available
at an overview.
It is very similar to the node selector, but it is more flexible as well as expressive.
For example, let's say that you have a requirement where you want to run this app a pod in any size
node except micro.
So here you have three nodes that are available micro medium, large.
You want to run this pod in any node except this micro node.
So here what is happening.
Strict equality based condition is not being used that we generally add as part of node selector.
So this specific approach can easily be achieved if you are making use of node affinity.

--- Requests and Limits ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about request and limits in Kubernetes.
Now again this is an important topic specifically when it comes to the production environment.
So let's go ahead and understand it.
So first we are going to explore few challenges post which we will be discussing on how this specific
feature allows us to overcome them.
Now the first challenge here states that a specific pod that is scheduled in a worker node can consume
more resources than expected, which will affect all of the other pods that are part of the same node.
So let's assume that you have a pod, you have app B bot, and suddenly you also have a app C pod.
But this pod is consuming a lot of Ram.
It is consuming a lot of CPU as part of the worker node.
Now what the issue will happen is that since this worker node has a finite amount of memory and finite
amount of CPU, if app C pod is consuming most of the Ram and CPU, then app A and app B pod will not
really get enough resources and this will in turn affect the overall production environment.
So ideally this is something that you do not really want.
And this is also one of the common things that you will see in production environments if the requests
and limits are not really set.
Now the second part here states that a pod requires certain amount of memory and computing resource
to run properly.
And this is expected.
So let's assume that app C pod requires 512 MB of Ram and two core CPU to run optimally.
Now, how will you tell Kubernetes that app C pod requires this much amount of Ram and this much amount
of CPU?
And based on this requirement, Kubernetes should schedule the pod accordingly.
Now, in a very simplistic terms, what you can do is you can go ahead and maybe assign a simple label
to the nodes and use the node selector to go ahead and create the pod in the largest node.
But this is something that does not really work well specifically when you have thousands of worker
nodes.
So you need to be able to clearly state the memory as well as the CPU related requirement to Kubernetes.
And Kubernetes can go ahead and look into all of the hundreds or thousands of worker nodes and then
schedule the pod accordingly.
So in order to overcome these two specific challenges that we were discussing, requests and limits
proves to be very useful.
So at a high level overview, using the requests and limits, you can control the amount of resource
that can be assigned to the pod, and also the appropriate node in which a pod can be launched.
For example, you have a request and you have a limit request is more of a guaranteed scenario.
Let's say that your pod really requires 256 MB of Ram to run.
If it does not really get this much amount of memory, it will not really work properly.
So this is part of a guaranteed memory.
So this is what the request is.
Limit is what is the maximum number of memory that a pod can consume.
I know that my pod requires Request 256 MB.
But what happens if it suddenly starts to use a lot of memory in a node?
So in order to control the maximum memory that a pod can use, you make use of limit.
So just for simplicity, I have also added a table here.
So when we discuss about the request, it denotes the minimum amount of CPU or memory a container is
guaranteed to get.
And based on the amount of CPU and memory that you add as part of the request, the Kubernetes will
assign the appropriate node that has enough resources to match the request related constraints.
In a similar way, when we discuss about limits.
Limit determines the maximum amount of CPU or memory that container is allowed to use.
In case if it uses more, then it can be throttled or the container can be killed.

--- Priority Class ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to go ahead and discuss about the priority class in Kubernetes.
Now one thing that we have to keep a note of is that in Kubernetes, pods can also have priority.
And based on the priority that you assign to a pod, it indicates to the Kubernetes the importance of
that pod in relative to the other pods that are running in the same cluster.
So in such cases, in case if a pod cannot be scheduled, the scheduler tries to preempt, which is
the lower priority pods to make the scheduling of the pending pod possible.
Now let's understand this through the diagram where you have the random pod and you have a critical
pod.
And let's say that you are trying to schedule one more important pod called as production pod into your
cluster.
Now, your cluster can only run two pods at a time.
Now, since this is an important pod manually, what is the pod that you will remove?
Will you remove the random pod so that the production pod can be scheduled?
Or you will remove the critical pod?
And the answer is yes.
manually.
You will remove or delete the random port so that the server has the appropriate capacity for the production
port to be scheduled.
Now, in a similar way, using the priority class, you can assign the priority to the individual port,
and based on the priority, Kubernetes can make the decision to remove the lower priority pods so that
the higher priority pods can be scheduled as part of the cluster.
Now, when we discuss about the advantages of the priority class, there are two important areas that
it influences.
One is the scheduling order.
In this case, the pods that has the higher priority are placed ahead in the scheduling queue.
So this is one part.
The second important area is the preemption.
So in case if the higher priority pods cannot be scheduled due to worker node not having insufficient
resources, then in such case, your scheduler can remove the lower priority pods from your cluster
so that the higher priority pods can be scheduled.
So with this base set, let's go ahead and look into how we can implement it.
Now, the first important object that you will have to create is the priority class object.
So again a very simple manifest file.
The kind is priority class.
The name associated with it is high priority.
And this has a value in this case 1000.
Now this value is important.
We'll be discussing why.
However note that 1000 is not the only value or the maximum value that can be added.
The priority class object can have any 32 bit integer value which is smaller than or equal to 1 billion.
So the possibilities here are quite high.
Now, once you have created this priority class object of higher priority and there is a value that
is assigned to it.
Now whenever you create a pod, you can assign the pod to this high priority class.
So in the second step you will be creating a pod.
And within the pod you can specify the priority class name.
In this case it is high priority.
So this will inform Kubernetes that this is going to be a higher priority pod.
pot, and it should be given priority both at a scheduling level as well as the preemption level.

--- Multi-Container POD Design Patterns ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
So in today's video, we'll be discussing about the Multi-container pod patterns.
Now, one of the first thing that you need to be aware is the sidecar pattern.
So the sidecar pattern is nothing but running multiple containers as part of a pod in a single node.
Now a single pod can contain multiple containers within it.
So this can also be better explained with this diagram over here.
And the similar diagram is used within the official documentation where this circle is a pod and this
pod has two containers.
The first container is the file puller, and the second container is the web server.
And you also have a volume which is being used by both of these containers to share the resources.
All right.
So this kind of a pattern is also referred as a sidecar pattern.
Now, this sidecar pattern can be better explained with this photo over here.
I'm sure many of you might have seen it where you have a scooter over here and this scooty is attached
to a sidecar.
Now, when you move this, both of these together are connected and they'll go together as well.
Similarly, a pod which has multiple containers.
So currently you see you have multiple containers.
So whenever you deploy this pod in any node, they will go together and they are connected with each
other.
So that is also referred as the sidecar pattern.
Now the next thing that you need to know is the ambassador pattern.
Now ambassador pattern is a type of sidecar pattern only where the second container is primarily used
to proxy the request.
Now again, if you see you have a pod over here and this pod has two containers.
Now, this proxy server on the right hand side, it acts as a sidecar.
And the main aim of this is to proxy the request from application server.
So let's say that the application server wants to connect to DB servers.
So what we do, the application server will send a request to the proxy server.
Proxy server in turn sends the request to the DB servers.
So any pattern of sidecar which is primarily used to proxy the request is called as the ambassador pattern.
Now in the sidecar pattern example, we had two containers.
One was file puller and second was web server.
Now let's say you had a web server and a proxy server.
So that kind of architectural pattern, although it is similar to a sidecar, is referred as the ambassador
pattern.
Now the next pattern is called as the adapter pattern.
Now adapter pattern is generally used to transform the application output in order to standardize or
normalize it for the aggregation.
So let's say that you have a container application based on PHP and it is writing the data in a specific
format.
Now what you need is tomorrow you need a different format.
So you want to interchange this fields and also add certain more fields.
So currently you see you have one more field called as PHP that you want to append it at the start.
So if you want to append it, you do not really want to modify your application container for it.
What you can do, you can introduce one more container called as the adapter container and this adapter
containers main job is to transform your logs so any logs with your application container is storing
in a volume.
This logs will be accessed by the adapter container and it will be modified according to the rules that
you had set within the adapter container.
All right.
So you can have various applications like Fluentd, which generally works in this pattern to transform

--- Init Containers ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the init containers.
So at a high level overview.
Init containers are the specialized containers that run before the application containers inside a pod.
Now let's understand this with a simple use case where you have a pod and you have a external storage.
And inside the pod you have a app container.
Now this app container is designed to run your application.
Now this application requires certain files that are part of the external storage.
Now for this, what you'll have to do as part of the app container, you'll have to create one more
logic which will first connect to the external storage.
Authenticate to the external storage may be using secrets, using TLS certificates, etc. and then fetch
the appropriate files.
And on top of that files it can go ahead and process the data.
Now the issue here is that apart from your main application, you are also configuring one more small
application or one more small logic that connects to the external storage may be external storage might
be using some different protocol.
So all of the logic you'll have to add as part of your application then authentication related data.
Also you have to add as part of the application and so on.
So this is something that you do not really want.
You want to keep your life simple.
And this is the reason why.
Application container.
You will leave it as it is.
The main focus of the application container is to run the application and that is what it will do.
Now in such cases, you will have one more container called as the init container.
Now this init container can contain all of the necessary logic to connect to the external storage,
authenticate to it, and fetch the appropriate files.
Now, since these are two separate containers in a single pod, you will need to share the data, right?
Because init container, once it fetches the data from an external storage, it has to make it available
for the app container.
So in such cases you can have a shared volume.
It can also be an empty volume since they are part of the single pod.
And then init container can authenticate to the external storage using the appropriate protocol, and
fetch the latest reports from here.
Once it fetches, it will store it inside the shared volume.
And then the application container can go ahead and connect to the data, read it and analyze and process
the data accordingly.
Now this shared volume ideally would be mounted both at a init container level as well as the app container
level as part of the pods.
All right.
So this is the basic high level overview about the init containers.
Now when we look into the workflow it would look something similar to this.
So you have a Kubelet and you have the actual app container.
Now when init container is configured the Kubelet will first go ahead and start the init container.
It will wait for whatever task the init container was configured for.
It will ensure that it runs to completion.
Then you have one more init container.
It will also start it.
It will run to completion.
Once that is done then it will start the actual app container.
All right.
So this is the high level workflow.
Now before we start the practical few important pointers we have to keep a note of.
First one is that init containers are very similar to the regular containers that you add as part of
the podspec, except first one is that init containers always run to completion, so the logic that
you add as part of the init containers needs to be completed.
Second is each init container must complete successfully before the next one starts, so a single pod
can have multiple set of init containers based on the requirement.
And the last important pointer is that in case if a pods init container fails, the kubelet will repeatedly
restart that init container until it succeeds again.
This depends upon the restart policy.
If you're using the default restart policy, which is always this is the behavior.
So with this we set.

--- Overview of Kubernetes Service ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about a very important topic in Kubernetes which is service.
Service is one of the common things that you will be implementing as part of the production environments.
So it is important for us to understand this topic in detail with full attention.
So with this, let's get started.
Now before we discuss about service, few pointers that we have to keep a note of.
First one is that whenever you create a pod in the Kubernetes cluster, the pod gets scheduled in the
appropriate worker node.
And it also has its own set of private IP address associated with it.
And the second point to note is that the pods that are part of the same cluster can communicate with
each other using these set of private IP.
So let's understand this with a simple diagram where you have a worker node and you have a front end
pod.
This front end pod, when it gets created it will have its own set of private IP address.
And then you have a back end pod.
Back end pod will also have its own set of private IP address.
Now let's assume that both of them are part of the same Kubernetes cluster.
Then both of them will be able to communicate with each other using the private IP address.
Let me also quickly show you a small demo so that this concept is understood.
Before we proceed further.

You can say kubectl get pods with the output of wide.
When you do a wide this is the one that we are interested in which is the IP address.
These are the private IP address that gets assigned to the pod.
Now similar to the diagram as we were discussing, generally, even in real world environment you will
have some kind of a front end.
And front end will receive the request from the client, and it will forward it to the back end pod
in a similar way.
Even in this diagram, we have a front end port.
We have a back end port.
And since both of them have a private IP and they are part of the same cluster, they will be able to
communicate using private IP.

Now, discussing about a common use case that you will also see in organization, where you will have
a front end port and this front end port, or maybe front end service needs to communicate with the
back end service.
Now let's assume that the IP address of back end port is ten 2440.5.
Now, since the communication needs to happen from front end to back end, and if you hardcode the IP
address of the backend port in the front end port configuration, it will work, but in the longer term
it will create issue.
For example, let's say in the configuration file of the application running in front end port, you
specify backend is this specific IP, so it will forward the request to the backend port.
Everything will work perfectly well.
But let's assume that after two months this backend port is having some issues.
So Kubernetes removed this specific backend port.
It deleted this backend port, and in a worker node to a new backend port got created.
So now what will happen?
Any request that goes to the front end port will fail.
Why?
Because front end port is trying to send the request to the backend port with the IP address that does
not really exist.
So now you'll have to update the Update the configuration of the front end pod with the newer IP address
of the backend pods.
So these pods are generally ephemeral, and you should never hardcode the IP address in the configuration
files.
Along with that, one more common challenge that you will see in organizations is that the pods generally
run as part of deployment.
So if you see over here, you have multiple set of back end pods that are running as part of the deployment.
And in this specific diagram you have three pods.
But if you have a large production website, it can be hundreds of pods that would be running in a deployment.
So again, if you are trying to hardcode the IP address of all of the pods as part of the deployment
in the configuration of the front end pod, this is something that is not really practical.
So this is one challenge.
Second challenge as we know deployment can go ahead and create new pods removing the previous pods that
are not working.
So this IP address they regularly keep on changing.
So hard coding is out of the question.
Along with that, you also want the front end pod to go ahead and distribute the request across the
back end pod.
You do not want front end pod to send 100% of the request to back end one pod, so the request should
also be equally distributed.
So this kind of logic must also be present in the application that is running in the front end pod.
So in order to overcome these set of challenges, as well as many other challenges in Kubernetes, you
have a feature of service.
So at a high level overview service acts as a gateway that distributes the incoming traffic between
its endpoints.
So now what will happen is since it acts as a gateway between a front end pod and the back end pod,
there is one more layer of service that comes into picture.
Now this service is very good with wide set of features like it can distribute the traffic across all
of these pods.
It can fetch the latest pods that are running as part of deployments, Etc..
So now, since this service has come into picture, all that front end pod has to do is that it needs
to send a request to the service, and service will take care of everything.
So ultimately, in the configuration file of the front end pod, you have to specify the backend which
is service dot internal so that the traffic goes to the service and let service take care of the rest.

Alright, so I hope with this at a high level overview, you understood the basics of gateway.
Not only it acts as a centralized point to receive the request, but it will also load balance the requests

Now, the second pointer that we have to keep a note is related to service and deployments.

--- Using Selector to Register Service Endpoints ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video, we are going to discuss on how we can use selector for registering the service
endpoints.
Now before we do that, one point that we need to note is that when you go through a very simple manual
based workflow to create a service, there are two steps.
First is you just create a simple service without any endpoints, and after you create a service, then
you can go ahead and manually add the appropriate endpoints that contains the IP address of the back
end port and associate it with your service.
So it will look something similar to this.
So first you go ahead and create a simple service.
You see this service does not really have any endpoints.
And once your basic service is created then you create an endpoint.
This endpoint contains the IP address that will be registered as the service endpoints.
So after both of these steps are completed, whenever a request is made to this simple service, that
request will be forwarded to this specific IP address.
Now, the issue with this specific approach, as we know, is that hard coding is required.
And in an environment where deployments are used.
When new pods come up every other day, the older pods get removed.
This manual hardcoding of IP address as the service endpoint is not really suitable.
So in such approach, there is one more better way of using selectors that works pretty well.
So in this approach, what happens is instead of hard coding the endpoints, you use the appropriate
selector.
So for example in this service manifest you have added a selector.
And what is the selector app equals to back end.
So now all of the pods that has this appropriate label the IP address of the pods will be registered
as the service endpoints.
For example if you have these two back end pods then this will be added as a service endpoint only and
only if it has the appropriate label of app as back end.
If it has a different label, it will not be added as the service endpoint.
And this is one of the quick ways in which you can add multiple set of pods as part of the service endpoints.
So let's also go ahead and try it out.

So this external world can also mean internet.
For example, when you create a base service based on cluster IP, you cannot access that service from
the internet because it has the internal IP only.

One of the common one used is node port.

Now, whenever you create a service of type node port, Kubernetes will assign a port from a node port
range.
So this is the range and this port will get assigned on all of the nodes in the cluster, which are
the worker nodes.
For example, you have a worker node.
Over here you have a external user.
So whenever you create a node port service, there will be a node port that will be assigned on every
worker node.
So now what external user needs to do.
External user needs to send a traffic to the worker node IP which should be a public IP if it is the
internet followed by the node port.
So when a request is made to the worker node public IP followed by the node port, then the request
is automatically forwarded to the appropriate service, and service will in turn forward it to the back
end ports.
All right.
So this specific part that you see where a port is open on all of the worker node.

--- Service Type - LoadBalancer ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
Today we are going to explore one of the very important service types in Kubernetes which is load balancer.
Now generally in production environments when you have a public facing application, this is the service
type that you will extensively be working with.
So with this let's get started.
Now before we explore the load balancer service type, it is important for us to understand what are
the challenges associated with the node port, because ultimately, even node port service allowed us
to expose our application to the external environment like internet.
Now, the main challenge here is that the user had to connect to the worker nodes IP address using this
node port like 31514.
Or it can be any other node port.
Now imagine you are connecting google.com not only with the DNS, but say google.com with 31210.
So this is so hard to remember.
No one is going to use it.
All right.
So even though node port is quite decent to expose the expose the application, but still it is not
really good for the production level environments.
And this is the reason why load balancer service type comes into picture.
So at a high level overview this service type, it sits between the external user and your node port.
So what happens you have a load balancer service types which creates a load balancer in your cloud provider.
And then external user using your website name can connect to the load balancer.
Load balancer in turn will forward the request to the appropriate node port, which then will forward
the request to the appropriate backend port.
Alright, so this is the basic architecture.
Let's go ahead and look into it from demo perspective.
Now for today's demo I already have a load balancer service that is created.
So when I do kubectl get service you see I have a service with a type of load balancer.
Now note that within here when you see external IP, this IP address is not of the worker node.
This IP address is of the load balancer.
So when I copy this IP address and when I do a curl, you see the website is working perfectly well.
Similarly if I add it in the browser you see we are getting welcome to nginx.
So now you don't really have to add a node port.
It is taken care by the load balancer service.
Now again we are using IP address.
But in the production environment you can have a DNS.
So you can use DNS like Labskin etc. and it will take to the appropriate website.
All right so I hope with this you understood the importance of load balancer service type.
Now one point to note, even in the diagram you can see even though node balancer service type is used,
but still there is a node port that you see in the worker node.
So this is one point that you have to keep a note which states that the load balancer service type automatically
creates a nodeport service.
Behind the scenes.
So if you see you have a service.
The type is load balancer.
However, this service also has a node port of 31249.
So ultimately the external load balancer whatever gets created.
It will receive the traffic and it will send to the appropriate node port of the worker node.
In fact, you can even see over here this ELB service that we have with the type of load balancer.
This service also has this node port.
So in fact if I have to show you you can say kubectl describe service elb service.
So within here if you will see this is the node port.
And then you also have the load balancer ingress.
So this is basically the load balancer related IPS over here.
Now the next very important point to note is that this service works only with the supported cloud provider.
Now in case if you have a on premise or a custom setup based on Kubernetes, additional configuration
is required.
It is not that it will randomly create a load balancer in any environment.
So only the supported cloud providers is where this specific will work.
So again AWS is very common.
AWS has a elastic load balancer.
DigitalOcean also has a load balancer.
Similarly, all of the major cloud providers where load balancer is available, this service will work
there.
However, let's say you are running it in minikube.
In such cases, it will not really work because ultimately Kubernetes also needs to connect to the cloud
provider so that integration will not be present if you are running it in a local setup like minikube.
However, if you are using a managed Kubernetes cluster, the managed Kubernetes cluster of a specific
provider already has the appropriate integration so that the load balancer can get created automatically.
For example, when we discuss about this specific service.
When this service gets created automatically in DigitalOcean, it also creates a load balancer.
If you see this is the load balancer that this service has created.
And when I open this load balancer, let's look into settings.

--- Overview of Ingress ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to go ahead and discuss about Kubernetes Ingress.
Now before we do that, it is important for us to understand the challenge that organizations face when
they have a simplistic configuration of a single load balancer service type.
Now, in this case, you will see that we have a very standard architecture.
You have a service.
This service is of type load balancer.
And this is the reason why the node port is also open.
So when an external user sends a request to the load balancer, a load balancer will in turn send a
request to the node port.
And then from the service it goes to the appropriate ports.
However, this type of architecture primarily supports a single service over here.
Now, in a larger organization, you will have multiple websites that might be hosted as part of Kubernetes.
So for each website you will have a separate service.
Now if you see you have an example service you have a service.
Each has their own individual pods.
Now in this case let's assume that whatever website configuration is part of the individual pod needs
to be accessible over the internet.
So what you do, you create a service with a type of load balancer.
Now in a basic configuration what will happen is each load balancer will be associated with a single
service.
So in this case if say example internal base request hits the load balancer it will go to the example
service.
And CP labs internal request hits the second load balancer.
It will go to the CP lab service.
Now if you have a single or 2 or 3 services this is fine.
But what happens if you have 4050 different websites that are part of your Kubernetes cluster?
Are you going to go ahead and launch 4050 different load balancers?
The answer is yes, you can.
But the load balancer management will become very difficult.
And also load balancers are not cheap.
They are quite expensive specifically for the providers like AWS.
So this is the reason why a little better architecture is required to deal with larger scale services.
So in the ideal approach, what you would like is you would like to have a single load balancer.
And this single load balancer should be able to handle requests for all of the services.
So what will happen is whenever a load balancer receives a request, for example based on the domain
of example internal, then based on the rules that might be configured, this request will automatically
go to the example service.
And similarly, if the request comes for internal it will go to the lab service.
So this is the ideal approach where a single load balancer should be able to handle requests for all
of the services.
And there should be a logic that routes the traffic accordingly.
So this specific rules and logic that we discuss is achievable using the Kubernetes ingress at a high
level.
Overview.
Ingress acts as an entry point that routes the traffic to services based on the rules that you define.
So within here you will have a ingress that comes into picture and then you have a load balancer.
Now when a load balancer sends a request to the ingress, the ingress component here will check for
what website the request is received.
In this case it has received the request for example dot internal.
So ingress based on the rules that are configured it will go ahead and forward this specific request
to example service.
