--- Ingress Rules - Routing Patterns ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss about different routing patterns that you can add as part
of your ingress rules.
Now, one of the common ones that you will be using regularly is related to name based virtual hosting.
In this case, the traffic is routed based on the host header as part of the HTTP request.
So this is specifically used when you have multiple set of services and multiple set of websites that
are hosted as part of the Kubernetes cluster.
For example, if you see if the host header has example dot internal.
So when someone types example dot internal in the browser, the browser will automatically add the host
header of the domain.
So in this case the request gets routed to service one.
If the domain is dot internal, the request gets routed to service two.
All right.
So as we are discussing this is one of the very common approaches for creating ingress rules.
And in fact, if you look into the Kubernetes documentation related to ingress, and if you search for
name based virtual hosting, this is where you will also get the basic example over here where you have
a host.
This is the first host.
This is the second host.
And the first host is sending traffic to service.
One second host is sending traffic to service two.
The second type is a path based routing where the traffic is routed based on the URL path in the HTTP
request.
So here you see you have app one which goes to app one, service slash app two which goes to app two
service.
And here also note that different path on the same hostname can point to different backend services,
right?
So this is the reason why the path based routing can also prove to be useful in a wide variety of scenarios.
Now, just for reference, I have also added a screenshot of the manifest file that demonstrates the
path based routing concept.
So here if you see you have a path of app hyphen one, and whenever a request comes to this path, it
goes to app hyphen one service.
And you have one more path of app hyphen two.
Whenever a request comes to this path it goes to app hyphen two service.
One more thing that needs to be noted here is there is no host specific field.
So irrespective of what is present as part of the host header, it does not really matter.
What matters here is the path.
So when you go ahead and create a service based on this manifest, the host will be star.

Now discussing about path type in Kubernetes, there are two primary ones that are available.
One is exact and second one is prefix.
So these are the important ones.
So exact matches the URL path exactly and is case sensitive.
So if you specify slash foo bar it only matches this specific one.
And when we discuss about prefix it is not exact.
So slash foo that you add in the path it will match slash foo.
It will also match slash foo slash.
So I have also added a screenshot that demonstrates more in detail on how that works.
So if you see in the kind you have a prefix, you have a exact.
For example, in exact.
If you specify slash foo and the request path is slash bar, it will not match.
This is simple to understand.
However, if you add slash foo but the request path is slash foo slash, so this additional trailing
slash is added.
Still, it will not match.
However, if you have a path type of prefix with slash foo then it will match slash foo.
It will match slash foo slash as well.
So depending upon what exactly you want to mix and match.
You have to use the appropriate path type accordingly.

--- Overview of Helm ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
Now, in today's video, we will be discussing about one of the very important topics in Kubernetes,
specifically when you're working in a production environment.
And the name of the topic is Helm.
So let's get started now at a high level overview.
Helm is one of the package manager for Kubernetes.
Now, at this stage, we have been working at multiple Kubernetes objects individually, like we have
been working with deployments.
Maybe we have been working with config maps, volume secrets.
ET cetera.
Now, when you work at an individual level, it is fine.
It is very straightforward.
However, in production environments, when you discuss about an application, an application might
use a lot of Kubernetes based objects.
It can use deployment secrets.
It can make use of a ingress controller volumes, it can make use of config maps and various others.
Now let's say that you have an application A and this application A is using so many Kubernetes objects
here.
Now you will not go ahead and deploy each one of these objects individually.
It will be a bit of a pain.
So what do you do in production environment?
You combine all of the objects that you will be creating as part of the application together, and this
is referred to as a helm chart.
So you have a helm chart of application A, and this chart has all of the Kubernetes objects required
to deploy and make sure the application A is up and running.
Now what do you do?
You go ahead and deploy this helm chart to your Kubernetes cluster.
Now you can have one Kubernetes cluster, two Kubernetes cluster, 100 Kubernetes cluster.
It does not really matter once you have all of the objects defined in a helm chart using your helm client,
you can deploy it to X amount of Kubernetes cluster, and that's about it.
This is how easy it is to deploy your entire application in production environment.
Now, one of the great things about Helm chart is the repository.
Now this application that we have been defining, this application can be created by you.
It can also be created by different organization altogether.
Let's say that you want to deploy a WordPress based blog on your Kubernetes cluster.
Now if you look into various public repositories available for Helm, there will be a WordPress chart
that might already be available.
So what you can do, you can simply make use of this WordPress chart and deploy it within your Kubernetes
cluster and your WordPress blog is up and running.
You do not really need to do anything here.
Similarly, there might be a Jenkins chart that might be available in a public repository.
Just take this chart, deploy it in your Kubernetes server and your Jenkins up and running.
So this is the great benefit of Helm.
So let's do one thing.
Let's go ahead and quickly try it out.
Now, currently I'm in a website of artifact hub.
So basically within here you can browse various helm packages that are available in various public repository.
Now, for example, let's say that I want to deploy MySQL within Kubernetes, so I'll search for MySQL
and you will see that there are multiple helm charts that are available from different set of providers
tomorrow.
I want to go ahead and deploy Jenkins I can search for Jenkins and you see officially from Jenkins,
I have a helm chart that is available and using this helm chart, I can directly deploy it in my production
environment.
So now at this stage, if Jenkins creates deployment secrets configmaps volumes, we do not really need
to worry.
All we have to do is we have to take this chart using helm and deploy it within the Kubernetes cluster.
That's how easy it is.
So for today's demo, we'll be deploying a WordPress chart, which again is available in the Artifact
Hub.
Let me quickly show you.

easy it is.

and the provider is Bitnami.

--- Kubernetes Namespace - New ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.

is namespaces.
So in production environment you will be using namespaces quite extensively.
So let's go ahead and understand what this is all about.
Now at a very high level overview using namespaces you can isolate a group of resources within a single
Kubernetes cluster.
For example, in this specific image you will see that you have a single Kubernetes cluster.
This Kubernetes cluster has multiple namespace development, staging, and QA, and each namespace has
their own individual resources like pods Configmaps secrets for each environment over here.
Now, before we go ahead and look into it from a practical perspective, let's look into the benefits
that this kind of architecture provides.
Now, in a Kubernetes cluster, it is not necessary that only one team might be working.
There can be multiple teams or multiple set of projects that share the same cluster.
And in such cases, when you have multiple teams, multiple projects.
Each team can have hundreds of pods in the larger environments.
So what you want is you want all of them within the same cluster, but they should not be interfering
with each other.
So using namespaces, it allows you to separate the environments like development, QA, staging as
part of a single Kubernetes cluster.

--- Named Port ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
Now, in today's video, we'll be discussing about the named port.
Now, whenever we are writing a specification for a port where a specific port is exposed, you would
know that the specification looks something similar to this, where under the spec containers we specify
port, and under that we specify container port followed by the port that needs to be exposed.
Now this is the regular approach.
Along with this, you can also associate a name for this port.
So here, along with the container port, you have also associated a name of Http.
So this is what is referred as the named port.
Now, one of the question that comes is what is the use for this specific named port?
So let's quickly find it out.
Now, one of the benefits of named port is that it can be referenced within the service file.
Now, if you look into this spec section, so this is a spec section of a service file.
So if you see this is a node port based service.
Now on the port side, we have specified port 80.
However, on the target port, we have specified Http instead of a port over here.
So if you see over here associated with this Http name port, you have a container port of 80.
So even though if you specify under the target port Http, things will work perfectly well.
So this is what is one of the benefit of named port.
So let's quickly jump into practical and understand on how it works.
So I'm in the CLI.
So in the first use case, let's quickly create a pod with the name of Nginx.
The image of Nginx will specify a port of 80 over here.
And let's quickly do a dry run of client and the output of Yaml.
So this is how it looks like.
So under the spec section, if you see you have a container port, but there is no name that is associated
with it.
So we'll intentionally go ahead and create a pod without a named port over here.
Now along with this pod, we'll also create a service.
So let's do a cube.
Ctl Expose Pod.

--- Overview of Horizontal Pod Auto-Scaling ---

Harry one.
And welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the horizontal pod autoscaling in Kubernetes.
Now, one thing that we have to keep a note of is that workloads in Kubernetes clusters are not always
static, and the workloads can fluctuate based on the user demand, traffic spikes, or sometimes even
due to the computational requirements.
Let's take an example where you have certain set of users and when they visit some application or websites
that are hosted in Kubernetes, the traffic is redirected to the appropriate pod.
Now, when you have a single pod that is running, it can take certain level of traffic.
It cannot take millions of requests.
So let's say in the upcoming weeks, maybe during the weekend when the amount of traffic increases towards
the Kubernetes.
In such cases, what will happen is that this single pod might not be able to handle all of the traffic
in such case.
Ideally, what you would like to do is you would like to have multiple set of pods, preferably in multiple
set of worker nodes that can distribute the incoming traffic that Kubernetes receives.
and this way the overall user experience will be much more better.
Now, generally in providers like AWS and even in other providers, you have a dedicated service of
auto scaling.
What happens there when the number of requests or number of CPU utilization increases of an existing
application, then the cloud provider will automatically increase the number of servers to handle the
traffic.
In a similar way, even in Kubernetes, using the horizontal pod autoscaler, referred to as HPA, it
can automatically adjust the number of running pods as part of deployment based on certain factors like
the CPU utilization, the memory usage, or it can also be certain metrics.
So let's take an example where there are certain set of requests.
Kubernetes is able to handle it perfectly in a worker node where you have two set of pods that are running
now in the weekend or in the holiday season, when you have more number of requests and you know that
these requests might not be taken care by the existing pods that are running because they are already
overloaded with the other request.
Then using the Horizontal Pod autoscaler, you can go ahead and maybe in the different worker node,
multiple set of additional pods can be created and these requests can be distributed across the pods.
So this function of creating new set of pods based on certain metrics like CPU utilization, memory
usage, etc. is achieved using the horizontal Pod autoscaler feature.
Now, the overall architecture would look something similar to this, where you have a existing replica,
set or deployment that is created, and this deployment or replica set is managing certain number of
pods.
Now you also have a horizontal pod autoscaler that you have configured.
Now what this horizontal Pod autoscaler will do.
It will monitor the CPU or the memory usage or any custom metrics that you have configured.
And in case if the CPU utilization of, say, pod one and part two is 100%, then the horizontal Pod
autoscaler will automatically scale the deployment to increase the number of pods, so it will automatically
does the scale out operation, which is adding new pods when the resource usage increases.
This is one part and also when the CPU utilization of pod decreases.
So let's say you have Monday, and now the average CPU utilization is just 10% at a pod level.
So you do not really want more number of pods of that application to be running because unnecessarily
it will be consuming resources.
So in such case, horizontal pod autoscaler will also perform the scaling in, which is removing the
extra pods when the overall resource usage decreases.
So let's also quickly look into the overall HPA workflow.
So in this specific screenshot you see that at this stage you have a CPU utilization of say 2% and the
target is 50%, the minimum pod is one, maximum pod is three, and currently the replica is one.
That means there is only one pod that is running as part of the deployment called PHP Apache.
So now what this means is that the target utilization is 50%.
So if the consumption of the ports that are part of this PHP Apache deployment is 50% in terms of CPU
utilization, then the horizontal pod autoscaler will increase the number of pods up to the maximum
pods that you have configured, which is three.
So at this stage you see currently you have 2%, but suddenly the number of spike has increased.
So it has gone to 380%, it has gone to 902%, etc..
So as soon as the spike increased, you will see that the replica count has also increased.
So earlier it was one, so there was one pod that was running.
Now it is three.
So based on the target metric that you have configured, the pods have automatically been created.
Additionally this is one part.
Now below you see from 323% the load has decreased back to 2% over here.
And similar to that, the replica count has changed from 3 to 1.
So when the load increased, the number of pods increased.
When the load decreased, the additional pods that were created have also been removed.
So all of this can be achieved using the Horizontal Pod autoscaler.
So let's do one thing.
Let's have a quick demo so that this part becomes much more clear to us.
Now for today's video, if I quickly do a kubectl get pods over here currently you see I have one pod
that is running.
It is running as part of the deployment.
In fact, when I do kubectl get deployment, you see at this stage this is the deployment.
And from this deployment you have one pod that is created.
This is one part.
Along with that I also have the horizontal pod autoscaler that is configured.
Now you have 2% over here and you have 50% which is the target.
So when the target gets hit, then the horizontal pod autoscaler will increase the number of pods from
minimum pod, which is one that is currently running to the maximum number of pods that you have configured,
which is three replicas means there is only one port that is currently running out of maximum of three
ports.
And this is the reason.
Also, as we know, we only have one port that you see over here.
So what we are going to do, we are going to make multiple set of requests to the application that is
running as part of the port, and we'll see on how the horizontal pod autoscaler will add the number
of pods.
So what we are going to do, we are going to watch this so that any changes gets reflected over here.
And from the second terminal tab we are going to create one more pod that is going to send the request
to the application pod that is running and that request, because you are sending multiple set of requests,
the CPU utilization of the application pod will increase.
You see these are the requests that are being sent now if you look into the utilization.
So for example if I do kubectl top pods this is the utilization over here.

pods that are currently running.

Now one more point that we have to keep a note of is that the horizontal pod autoscaler does not apply
to objects that cannot be scaled like Daemonsets, so only the objects that can be scaled like replica
set deployments.
The horizontal Pod autoscaler will support that.

--- HPA - Stabilization Window ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss about the stabilization window as part of the Horizontal
Pod autoscaler configuration.
Now generally when we work with HPA, when we discuss about the scale up operation, it does not really
take too much time.
For example, here you see you have a deployment of PHP Apache.
Now you have 2% of 50%.
So 50% is the target utilization post which the horizontal pod autoscaler will increase the number of
pods.
Now, when the CPU utilization was less, the total number of pods that were created were just one.
Now slowly the number of utilization increased from 2%.
It increased to 380% and then it increased to 902%, etc..
Now as soon as it increased.
So here you had replica of one at 90s where the higher CPU load was detected, and then at 106 seconds,
which is approximately 16 seconds more, the number of replicas as part of the deployment were increased
to two three.
So this scale up operation did not really take much time.
Contrary to that, when you look a bit down at this stage, you see from 323%, the load decreased to
7% again.
Now since the load decreased, we would expect that the HPA will scale down the pods in a similar time
frame that it had used for the scale up operation.
So at two minutes 46 seconds the CPU utilization decreased.
The number of pods were still three.
Now at three minutes again you have three.
At seven minutes, 31 seconds.
Again you have three, and at seven minutes 46 seconds you have one.
So it took around five minutes for the scale down operation to take place.
However, scale up operation was pretty quick.
Now the question that comes is why exactly is this?
Now when we discuss about the production environments, note that sometimes the temporary metric drop
can create rapid scale down of the pods, which might cause the service instability.
Now, generally when you have higher number of pods than what are required for the end user perspective,
it is not really going to make any difference.
In fact, the website might be much more faster.
However, if the number of pods are lower, then the end user is going to get affected and this is something
that you do not really want.
And this is the reason.
By default, Kubernetes adds the stabilization window specific configuration that adds the delay before
the pods are downscaled.
So for upscale there is no delay.
For downscale, there is a delay.
And this in fact is suitable for the production environment perspective.
So at a high level overview the stabilization window configuration, it tells the HPA to wait for a
certain period of time before it can scale down.
Now when we look into the default stabilization window, the scale up is zero, so there is no delay
as part of the scale up operation.
However, scale down operation, there is a delay of 300 seconds, which is a five minute delay.
And this is something that we already saw as part of the screenshot as well.
Now both of them can be added as part of the HPA.
So for scale down, the default configuration as we know is 300 seconds.
For scale up it is zero seconds.
In case if you would like, you can go ahead and configure it based on the requirements as well.
Now once you have modified the stabilization window for scaling down operation from 300 seconds default
to 60s, you can observe the workflow now.
Now, similar to the first screenshot, initially you had one replica of the deployment.
Suddenly the load increased and in a moment you see from 38 seconds to 90s immediately.
Now you have five replicas as part of the deployment.
Now once the load decreased because from here at this stage, the load decreased from 712% to 2%.
So this happened at two minutes 30s and at three minutes 30s exactly after 60s the number of replicas
reduced from 5 to 1.
one.
So here you did not really have to wait for five minutes for the scaling down operation to complete
after you have modified the configuration here.
So let's go ahead and look into it so that this part can make better sense.
Now within the documentation of horizontal pod auto scaling, there is a specific area of stabilization
window as we are discussing.
And the main area here is the scale down.
And within here as we are discussing by default you have the 300 seconds.
So this is the default behavior.
In case if you would like you can go ahead and modify this based on the requirement.
Now in order to test it out first we are going to go ahead and quickly create a new deployment.
So let's go ahead and quickly create this deployment I'll copy this and I'll just paste it.
So it is basically the combination of service and deployment I'll save this.

--- Overview of Vertical Pod Auto-Scaler ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the Vertical Pod Autoscaler.
Now one thing that we have to keep a note of generally in production environments, you will see that
organizations will typically add the requests and limits as part of the pod manifest or the deployment
manifest, and in fact, this is a good practice.
However, one of the issues here is that in case if the developer or the administrator has set the request
and limits as part of the pod or the deployment manifest to too low, then in such cases, your app
might crash because your app will not really get the resources that it requires to run efficiently.
However, in case if you set the value to be too high, then you will be wasting the resources as part
of your cluster.
So specifically when we discuss about two high in such cases, even if your application is idle and
it is using very little CPU or memory, the requested amount that you might have added while creating
the resource, this requested amount is blocked off, and it cannot be used to schedule the other ports
onto the node.
So let's take an example where you have a worker node with three core and three GB Ram.
Now whenever you have created a pod.
Now for this pod, you have given a three core and three GB ram as a request.
So this is like a minimum.
However, Pod does not really require this much amount of resources.
Now the issue here is that although the pod got scheduled in the worker node, it is using way less
resource than it has requested.
However, since you have requested this as a minimum, this extra resources that is not being used,
this part will be blocked off.
So the scheduler will not really schedule other pods onto the node because this pod has requested for
the entire resources over here.
So ideally you would like a tool that will monitor the consumption of the CPU.
And based on that it can modify the request and maybe the limits to be adjusted accordingly in the production
environments.
And this is achieved using the Vertical Pod autoscaler.
At a high level overview, the VPA is the component that automatically adjusts the CPU and memory requests
for containers running within your pods.
So what it will do, it will give you the recommendation.
For example, the nginx container name.
This is the recommendation that it has been giving to you, and based on the recommendation, you can
either modify the request accordingly or if you want, the VPA can also do it for you in an automated
fashion.

Then it will make things much more clear.

Note that this is a demo video.

Now it can happen that the request is also too low or it can be too high.
Both the cases are available.
Now I also have a vertical port autoscaler that is available.
If you see I have a vertical port autoscaler that is available and this vertical pod autoscaler as we
know it can adjust the requests accordingly.
So let's do one thing.
Let's go ahead and create this specific nginx deployment.
Now from a different tab when you do kubectl get pods, you see we have two pods that are currently
running.
Now let's do one thing.
Let's go ahead and do kubectl get pods.
We'll watch this.
And meanwhile let's open this I'll do cube ctl describe pod.
We'll take one of the pods and we'll verify if you see the pod also has a request of CPU of 50 and memory
of 50 mi.
Now what the VPA will do is it will observe the overall utilization.
So it will require the metrics server.
It will observe the overall utilization.
And based on that it will adjust the request based on the optimal value.

And in fact you will also get the recommendation if you would like.
When I do kubectl describe vpa engine eks vpa within.

Alright, so I hope with this you understood the basics of the Vertical Pod autoscaler.
Now, before we conclude, one more pointer that I wanted to share specifically related to the update
mode for the VPC.
Now there are three primary update modes of initial and auto.
When you have update mode as of, VPA will only give you recommendations.
There will be no changes that would be applied in auto.
VPA actively applies the recommendation by evicting and restarting the pods.
So we saw on how some pods were getting terminated and new pods were getting created.
Why?
Because the VPA mode was auto.
You also have the initial mode, where VPI only assigns the resource request on pod creation and never
changes them later.
Now, let me in fact show you when you do kubectl get VPA you will see that here the mode is auto and
this was the reason why it was actually able to terminate the pod and the newer pods were recreated.
In case if the mode was set to off, it will only stick with the recommendation and it will not really
modify things.

--- Overview of Gateway API ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video at an overview, we are going to discuss about the gateway API.
Now one of the prerequisite for this specific video is your understanding about the ingress and the
ingress controller, because gateway API is related to them.
Now, just to revise, ingress is generally used to manage the external user access towards the services
as part of your cluster.
And again, this is quite common in the production environments.
Now if you'll quickly revise the basic workflow you have the ingress managed load balancer.
So client sends the request to the Ingress Managed Load balancer.
And from here the request is redirected towards the ingress and its associated objects.
Now within here you have certain set of rules based on the rules the traffic will be redirected to the
appropriate service.
Now again we had a detailed video on Ingress and Ingress controllers.
So make sure that you go ahead and watch that and ensure that your understanding is clear before proceeding
further.
Great.
Now, although ingress and egress controllers are used quite extensively in the production environments,
but it comes with its own set of limitations.
One of the primary limitations is that the ingress API primarily handles the HTTP and Https related
traffic.
Now for the production environments, you can have various other protocols as well, maybe TCP, UDP,
gRPC, and there are applications that work on those.
So just by using HTTP and Https protocols, you do not cater to all of the demands that the organizations
will have.
Along with that, the ingress also lacks native support for advanced traffic management features that
are generally required.
As part of the production scenarios.
We will be discussing about the second point in more detail once we understand the basics of gateway
API.
Now, at this stage, just note that there are certain limitations of ingress, and in order to overcome

layer seven protocols like TCP, UDP, you have HTTP, you also have gRPC, and there are many others
that are under the considerations.
This is one of the great benefits of gateway API when we compare it with the traditional ingress.

--- Structure of Gateway API ---

Everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss about the overall workflow structure and the components that
are part of the gateway API.
Now, the first point to note is that the gateway API includes the gateway class.
Then you have the gateway, then you have the protocol specific route, and then you have the actual
service associated with the application.
Now why do we mention protocol specific route?
Because gateway API supports various protocols at layer four which are TCP, UDP, as well as at layer
seven like HTTP gRPC.
Now within here, from the practical point of view, the gateway class, the gateway and route, these
are the three very important areas that we have to understand in detail in today's video.
We are going to look into it from the demo perspective.
And then in the upcoming videos when we do the practical, then it will make things much more clear.
Now, before we explore about each aspect in detail, let's quickly revise the workflow here.
So on the top you have the gateway class, you have the gateway, then you have the protocol specific
route, and then you have the underlying service that will direct to the appropriate application ports.
So first let's go ahead and discuss about the gateway class.
Now one point to note is that the gateways can be implemented by different controllers.
So there are multiple set of controllers that are available.
And gateway class specifies the controller used to implement the gateway API resources.
For example, if you see when you do cube CTL get gateway class, you have the controller.
In this case we are making use of nginx gateway controller.
Now is nginx the only controller that is available?
And the answer is no.

--- TLS Configuration - Gateway API ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss about TLS specific configurations as part of the gateway
API.
Now generally, whenever you want to work with TLS at a gateway API level, there are two connections
that you should know of.
One is the downstream.
So downstream is basically the connection between the client and the gateway.
So you have a client which can be the internet user.
So this connection between the client and the gateway because here also network is involved.
So when you discuss about TLS you have to identify what exactly do you want to achieve.
One is either the downstream so you can achieve encryption between client and gateway.
And then you have upstream.
So upstream is basically the connection between the gateway as well as the back end service.
Now whenever you work with TLS at a gateway API level, there are two important modes that you should
be aware of.
One is the TLS pass through mode.
Second is the TLS terminate mode.
The terminate mode is very simple where the encryption happens between the client and the gateway API.
So this downstream that we were discussing this can be achieved using the TLS terminate mode.
So what happens here is that since TLS is getting terminated at a gateway API level, the traffic from
client and gateway API will remain to be encrypted through the network.
And since TLS is getting terminated here, the traffic from the gateway API towards the appropriate
port will remain to be in the plain text format.
So here you have the HTTP, and in the downstream you have the Https.
The second is the TLS passthrough mode.
What happens here is that the connection does not get terminated at a gateway API level.
So this is referred to as the pass through.
This connection gets terminated directly at a port level over here.
So this is much more secure.
Now one more point to note is that in the TLS terminate mode, since the termination is happening at
a gateway API level, you will require the certificates.
And these certificates are managed at a gateway level.
However, in the passthrough mode, since the TLS termination is happening directly in the port, the
certificate and the appropriate private key must be as part of the pod over here.
Now, when you compare both of these approaches, as we are discussing in the TLS passthrough mode,
the decryption happens at a pod level.
And in the TLS termination mode, the decryption happens at a gateway level itself.
So whenever you enable TLS you have to decide which mode you want.
You either want a passthrough or you want the termination related mode.
Let's also discuss some of the pointers related to it as we are discussing.
The first point is that TLS decryption point in the passthrough, it gets decrypted at the back end
pod level indeterminate.
It gets decrypted at a gateway level.
Certificate management.
Also, since the TLS in the terminate mode is getting terminated at a pod level, the appropriate certificates
and the private key must be at a pod level.
In the terminate mode, it must be at a gateway level.
Now, few very important pointers here.
The content inspection.
When you use the passthrough mode, it is not really possible.
Also, when we discuss about some of the important features of gateway API, like the request modification,
if you want to modify the HTTP headers, if you want to work around with routing capability in more
detail, all of these will be blocked or limited when you use the TLS passthrough mode.
For example, as we were discussing that in the passthrough mode, since the request is still encrypted,
the gateway API will not be able to modify the HTTP headers.
It will not be able to perform the appropriate inspection of the request.
So this is one of the downside.
If the gateway API does not do the inspection, then the overall features will be quite limited when
compared to the terminate mode.
In the terminate mode, since the TLS is getting terminated at a gateway API level, the gateway API
can inspect modify the request, and it can also modify the HTTP headers based on the requirements.
So let's do one thing.
Let's have a quick demo of the TLS terminate mode, so that we understand on how exactly the workflow
would look like.
Now for today's video, if I'll quickly do a cube CTL get gateway, I have the gateway that is configured.
This is based on TLS.
So let me quickly show you when I quickly do a cube CTL describe gateway.
Let's look into the gateway.
Let's go a bit up.
So this is the important part that I wanted to show here.
If you see the mode here is terminate.
This is something that we just saw.
Now since this is dealing with the TLS as part of the listeners, the protocol would be Https.
This is very important.
And the port will be 443.
Now one more point that we were discussing that in the terminate mode, since the gateway API will be
responsible for decrypting the TLS from the client to the gateway API endpoint, the gateway API will
also require the certificate and the private key.
Otherwise it will not be able to decrypt.
So this certificate and private key is generally referenced or provided to the gateway API by adding
the appropriate Kubernetes secret based on type of TLS.
So let's also quickly revise this.
So when you explore the Kubernetes secrets here, one of the aspects here is the TLS secret.

key.

--- Mapping of Ingress API to Gateway API ---

Now, the first area that we need to keep a note of is related to the entry points.
Now, from the perspective of entry points, when we discuss about ingress, every ingress resource
has two implicit entry points.
One will be for HTTP and second will be for the Https based traffic.
And it is the ingress controller that will provide these entry points.
Now whenever you create an ingress now in this ingress you do not specify that I need ingress only for
HTTP, or I need it only for Https.
Even if you have not really specified anything as part of the ingress, by default the HTTP and https
will be enabled at the ingress controller level.
Now when we compare this with the gateway API, things are slightly different in gateway API.
The entry point must explicitly be defined as part of the gateway resource.
Now, if you will see as part of this gateway resource, you have a listener.
The protocol is HTTP and the port is 80.
So this part is important and you have to define it.
Now let's say that you have Https that is defined over here.
And then you send the traffic to the gateway API over HTTP protocol so that traffic will not be allowed.
This is the reason why in gateway API inside the gateway resource, you have to be very specific on
what needs to be allowed.

--- Helm - Skipping CRDs ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss on how you can skip the cards whenever you are installing
the helm chart.
Now, the first point to note is that with the helm three, there is now a special directory called
as Crds that you can create in your chart that holds the crds for you.
And in case many a times in organizations, in Kubernetes clusters, the crds already exist.
So in such cases, if you install the helm chart, these crds will be skipped with a warning.
However, if you want to explicitly skip the CRD installation, then you can pass the Skip Crds flag.
Now, one more point to note is that it is not necessary that if you use the skip Crds, the Crds will
not be configured.
It depends upon case to case basis and how the chart has been created.
So depending upon the chart, there can be different ways that might be possible to skip the crds.
For example, if you look into this chart, you have a custom resource definition.
And there is a specific condition over here which states that if values dot Crds dot install.
So if this is set to false, then.
Crds will not be installed.
However, if the default value of this is true, then Crds will be installed over here even if you go
ahead and use the skip Crds.
So this is one point to keep a note of.
Generally, what you can do if you want to be 100% sure, you can go ahead and create a helm template.
Set the appropriate approach to skip the crds and verify if the final YAML file has the CRD or not.
And this is one of the easy ways to verify.
Let's go ahead and try it out.
This will give us better clarity.
Now for today's practical we are going to take one example of Argo CD.
So within here let's search for all of the results.
So this is related to OCI.
We are more interested in the normal one.
So this is Argo project Argo.
Let's go ahead and open this.
Now within here you will get all of the information here.
One of the ways in which you can verify whether this specific helm chart is installing the Crds.
You can look into the source code.
For example, if you look into the helm over here in the GitHub.
Let's go to templates.
We'll go to say Crds.
And you see you have crds that are available.
And if you open this over here you have the Crds.
And for the installation of Crds you have a specific condition which is if values dot Crds dot install.
So if crds dot install let's say is set to true, the crds will get installed.

--- Authentication in Kubernetes ---

Now at a high level overview authentication is the process of verifying the user's identity before granting

In fact, this is something that all of us would know that if we log in to our laptops or desktop devices,
the first thing that it asks us is to supply the appropriate password.
So this is primarily what authentication is about.

one of the important things that we need to do is we have to authenticate first.
So let's say that you have a client over here and you have a Kubernetes cluster.

In an ideal scenario.

--- Authorization in Kubernetes ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about authorization in Kubernetes.
Now before we discuss about it, let's quickly revise the basics at a high level.
Overview.
Authorization is the process of determining what an authenticated user or entity is allowed to do.
Now let's assume that you have created a new AWS user.
Now, this new AWS user is trying to delete all of the servers that are running in the entire AWS account.
So the question is, should he be allowed to do that?
And the answer is it depends if he has a permissions or not.
If he has permission, he will be able to do that.
If he does not have permission, he will not be able to do that.
So this part of permissions is where authorization comes into picture.
Now in fact, let me also show you this from a high level overview.
So currently in AWS I have multiple users.
Now when we look into this specific test user over here, this user at this stage, you see, does not
really have any permission.
So in case if this user logs in to AWS and tries to delete the server, he will not be able to do that.
Why?
Because the user does not have any permission.
Now let's say that I want this user to be able to delete.
In such case, I'll have to explicitly add permission to this specific user.
For example, let's say that I want to add administrator permission for this user.
And now user will be able to perform all of the operations.
So this specific part that we just did of adding a permission for a specific user, this part is related
to the authorization.
Now when we discuss about it from the Kubernetes perspective, note that the authorization takes place
following the authentication.
So first part is always the authentication.
And then the authorization will come into picture.
All right.
So generally in idle scenario a client making a request must first be authenticated.
Whatever method, it does not really matter before the request can be allowed in the authorization phase.
So you have the authentication, you have the authorization, and you have the Kubernetes resource.
It can be pods, secrets, etc. these are the two major areas.
Now if this specific client wants to access this resource then the step number one in an ideal scenario
is the authentication.
If the user is successfully authenticated, will that mean that the user will be able to perform all
of the operations in Kubernetes?
Will he be able to delete all of the pods, fetch all of the secrets, etc.?
And the answer is it depends whether the user has the permission or not.
So after user authenticated using say X509 certificates or token, then the step number two is the authorization.
Authorization is the place where Kubernetes will determine whether this user who has authenticated has
permission on the Kubernetes resources or not.
And after authorization phase succeeds, then the request will go towards the Kubernetes resources.
If a user does not have permission, then it will be blocked at the authorization phase itself.
Now, in Kubernetes, there are a wide set of authorization modes that are available to suit multiple
set of environments.
Let's take example of three.
There are many, but we are taking example of three because we just want to understand this topic of
authorization at an overview.
Now you have three authorization mode always allow, always deny and Rbac three as part of this table.
Now always allow by the name itself.
We can determine that this mode allows all the requests.
So ultimately if a user is authenticated, he will not be denied at the authorization phase.
All of the operations that he is trying to perform will be allowed.
Second is always deny where this mode will block all of the of the requests.
And in fact, both of these modes that we were discussing are generally used only for testing.
They are not really used for production environments.
And the third very important authorization mode is related to Rbac.
Rbac is where we go ahead and set the permissions, and based on the permission policies, the access
will be granted.
So let's also have a quick demo to understand these.
Now one point to note is that this specific part that we were discussing, where we added the administrator
access this ultimately behind the scenes is a policy.
So Rbac that you see over here is something similar to this, where you have to go ahead and add the
appropriate permissions.
And based on the permission that you have defined the policy will either allow or block based on the
request when it reaches the authorization stage.

--- Role Based Access Control (RBAC) ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about the role based access control, also referred to
as Rbac.
Now within your Kubernetes cluster, if you have the Rbac based authorization mode enabled, it allows
us to control what actions specific entities like user groups service accounts can perform on the resources
within your cluster.
For example, whenever a request is made towards your Kubernetes cluster, the first important part
is authentication.
If authentication succeeds, and if you have the right authorization, and considering that you have
the authorization of Rbac, then at the Rbac level, there will be certain set of permissions based
on the permissions.
You will either be granted the access or you will be denied the access.
So let's look into it from the basic workflow perspective.
So within here you have a set of users like Alice Bob.
And then you also have set of permissions like list pods, create delete secrets etc..
So the first point states that in the below diagram here in the table one, you have a list of users.
And in the table two you have list of permissions.
Now these two are separate entities.
Altogether they are not really connected.
So you might have certain list of users.
You might have certain list of permissions.
But this does not really mean that the user of Alice and Bob will be associated with these specific
permissions.
So if you want that the user of Alice and Bob should get these specific permissions, then ultimately
you will have to bind them or you will have to connect them together.
Once you have these binded, then the users will get all of the permissions that are been listed over
here.
Now that we understand the basic conceptual workflow, let's go ahead and link it with three important
Kubernetes specific concepts.
First important one is the rule.
Now at a high level overview rule defines a set of permissions.
So here instead of permissions that we had in had in the earlier slide.
You have a role, and this role provides a certain set of permissions like list pods, create, delete
secrets, etc. then you have subjects.
These subjects can be users, groups or even service accounts.
And as we know, these two are independent at this stage.
Now if you want that these specific subjects, whatever it may be, are allowed to perform the actions
that are part of this role, then you will need a role binding.
What role binding does?
It connects the subjects to the role.
So once role binding is in place, then whatever permissions role has the subject will inherit those
specific permissions.
Now let's go ahead and discuss more in detail about role.
One very important point specific to role is that a role always sets the permission within a particular
namespace.
Now if you see you have a role definition and you have a permission like get pods, list namespaces,
create secrets, watch pod logs now.
Permissions.
You have good amount of flexibility.
What exactly you want the user or what exactly you want the group to be able to do.
Now, whatever this role has, this is always part of the namespace scope.
So you can create a role for say default namespace.
You can create one more role for a different namespace, etc..
And the second concept as we were discussing is the role binding, which associates the role with the
user groups or service account within a specific namespace.
Very important part to remember.
So for example, you have a create secrets permission as part of this role.
Now when this role is associated with a group of user, the group of users will be able to create a
secret only in a specific namespace.
They will not be able to create secrets in other namespace.
It is very specific to a namespace over here.
All right, so let's do one thing.
In today's video we are going to have a demo.
And in the upcoming videos we'll have a separate detailed practical so that we understand it properly.
However, today's video is a demo video.
Aim is to understand the concept.
Now for today's demo I have two tabs open in a custom Kubernetes cluster.
In the first tab, my kubectl is associated with the admin privileged user.
In the second tab, the cube ctl is associated with the user named Bob.
From the admin user over here, when I say kubectl get pods, we are seeing certain information now
from the Bob user.
When I say kubectl get pods, you see we are getting an error.
What is the error?
Error is forbidden.
Pods is forbidden.
User Bob cannot list the resource pods.
So this is clearly the permission issues.
Now, as we were discussing, when you want to give a permission as part of Rbac, the first thing that
you will require is a role.
Second thing you require is certain subjects like user.
And the third thing that you require is a role binding.
Now for this demo.
I already have a user of Bob, so the first part is done.
Remaining part is the role and the role binding.
Now from the server.
If I do a LHS we have few important files here.
One is the role, second one is the role binding.
You also have a cluster role and cluster role binding, which we will be discussing in just a moment.
Aim here is to understand this specific part first.

--- Introduction to Asymmetric Key Encryption ---

Huron.

In today's video, we will be discussing about the asymmetric key encryption.
Now, the asymmetric key cryptography makes use of public and private keys to encrypt and decrypt the
data.
So let's understand this in a simple way.
So what happens in asymmetric key encryption is that there are two keys which are involved, and these
two keys are in some way related with each other.
So what happens here is that whatever data that you encrypt with one key can only and only be decrypted
with the second key here.
And in a similar way, whatever data that you encrypt with, the second key can only be decrypted with
the first key.
So that's the basic concept of asymmetric key.
So here it is referred the two keys are referred as public key and private key.
So one key is public and second key is private.
Now, as the name suggests, the public key can be shared with everyone, so you can share it across
the Internet.
There is no issue there.
And the other key is kept as secret and you do not share it with anyone.
And it is called as the private key.
So as we discussed, either of the keys can be used to encrypt a message and the opposite key from the
one which is used to encrypt the message is used for decryption.
So let's understand this.

Her name is Alice.

a unsafe network.

--- emptyDir Volume ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the volume type of mtdr.
Now at a high level overview.
The empty volume is primarily used for temporary storage directory as part of the pod.
Now, one of the great benefits where empty volume is used quite extensively is specifically when you
have a Multi-container based pods and the containers wants to read and write on the same set of shared
files.
In such case, you can create an empty volume.
Now let's take an example where this is a pod.
You can consider this to be a multi container port where you have a writer container which will write
certain files, and you have a reader container which will read the files that have been written by
the writer container.
Now, since both of them wants to work on the same set of files, you will need a volume.
And in such case, empty dir volume proves to be important, so you can associate this empty volume
with both of the containers and the writer container can write the data in the empty volume reader container
can read the data from the empty data volume over here.
Now, before we start with the practicals, let's look into some of the key features of mkdir.
First important one is that it is deleted when the port is removed.
So this is a very important pointer to keep a note of.
So in case if you want that volume should not be removed once the ports are deleted, then you can choose
a different type of volumes that are available in Kubernetes.
But in case if you have a use case where this data in the volume is no longer required after pod is
deleted, then empty dir is quite good enough.
So this is the first important part.
Second is that the empty dir volume can also use memory instead of disk for performance, and memory
is way way faster when compared with the disk.
So this is important to note.
And next is a container.
Crashing does not remove a pod from the node.
So this is a point to note.
So the data in an empty volume is safe across the container crashes.
So this is also a point that you have to keep a note of.
Now, as we are discussing, empty volume can work both at a memory level, which is much more faster,
so the data will be stored in your memory or empty.
Deer can also store the data as part of your disk.

--- hostPath Volume ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the volume type of host path.
Now at a very high level overview the host path volume.
It mounts a file or directory from the host, which is the nodes file system into your pod, and this
is useful in a wide variety of use cases.
Let's take a simple example where you have a pod, and in the pod you have a single container.
Now this pod must be running somewhere, right?
So it would ideally be running on top of the worker node.
Now the worker node on which the pod is running this worker node will also have its own file system.
So using the host path what you can do is you can connect or you can mount the file system associated
with the host inside your pod.
And all of the files that are available as part of your worker node will be available inside the container
as well.
So this is useful in a wide variety of use cases.
First one is where if your container requires access to the worker node specific log files like var
log for analysis.
Now since var log Resides on the host.
Using the host path, you can mount this specific directory into your pod and can perform the required
level of analysis.
Second is if your container requires access to the worker node specific configuration files, so this
is also quite useful.
Third is where container that wants to write persistent data to a specific path in the worker node.
So in this specific worker node there is a directory.
And your pod wants to write all of the persistent information to the directory.
In such case, you can mount a directory from the worker node to your pod and then do the appropriate
level of writing.
So this is the basics of the host path based volume.
Let's go ahead and quickly try it out.
Now within the volumes documentation in Kubernetes, let's quickly look into the host path based volume
type.
So this is the host path based volume type.
And if you look into the basic manifest file this is how it looks like.
You have the volume and you have the volume mounts.
So I have taken the example and I have trimmed it down to the most essential aspects.
Now this part is something that we already know.
The volume mounts is also something that is easy to understand.
The only difference here is the volumes.
Now in the volumes over here, you can specify the name of the volume and the host path.
And this is the path of the worker node that you want to mount in your pod.
For example, in your worker node you have a directory of var log.
And let's say that you want this specific directory to be mounted inside your container, because container
wants to analyze the log files that are part of the worker node.
Then you can specify this path.
So this path is of that of the host.
And then you can specify in the volume mounts on which specific path the files that are part of the
var log should be mounted to.
All right.
So just for simplicity what we are going to do, we are going to set it to root.
So all of the root file system of the host will be mounted to the worker node data inside the pod.
All right.
So this is the basic host path based example.

--- Static vs Dynamic Provisioning of PV ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back in today's video, with respect to the persistent volumes, we are going
to discuss about the two important types of provisioning.
One is the static provisioning of persistent volume.
Second is the dynamic provisioning of persistent volumes.
So at this stage, note that when it comes to persistent volume, the first approach is the static provisioning.
In this case, the persistent volume must be created before you go ahead and create the persistent volume
claim.
So in this approach may be a storage administrator can manually create the persistent volume and keep
it ready.
Now the second approach, which is much more preferred in the production environment is the dynamic
provisioning.
In this case, the persistent volume need not be created by the storage administrator, and the PV will
be created dynamically whenever you create a PVC.
So this is much more, better and more efficient approach that a lot of organizations makes use of.
Let's go ahead and discuss about both of these in more detail.
Now, the first approach of static provisioning is something that we have already seen, in which the
administrator will go ahead and manually create the persistent volumes ahead of time.
So in this case, you have multiple persistent volumes that are created and the status is available.
So a user that wants to make use of the appropriate persistent volume will create the persistent volume
claim that can match the appropriate persistent volume, and the volumes will be assigned accordingly.
In case if there are no matching persistent volume exists, then the PVC will remain in the unbound
state.
This is very important part to note.
Let's take an example where you have two persistent volumes of size one GB and three GB.
Now a user has created a persistent volume claim of ten GB.
Now there are no persistent volume to match that.
So in such cases that PVC will remain in the unbound and pending state because there are no persistent
volumes that are available.
This is also one of the disadvantages of static provisioning.
The much more better approach is the dynamic provisioning.
In this case, you do not really have to create a persistent volume at all.
Whenever a persistent volume claim is requested by the user.
Automatically Kubernetes will create the appropriate persistent volume here.
And this is done using one important object called as the storage class.
So if you see there is a persistent volume claim this time, and this persistent volume claim is associated
with a storage class of do block storage.

--- Reclaim Policy for Persistent Volumes ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video specifically related to the persistent volumes, we are going to discuss about the
reclaim policies.
Now at a very high level overview of reclaim policy, it specifies what happens to a persistent volume
and its underlying storage after the associated PVC is deleted.
Let's understand it through a diagram where you have a persistent volume claim.
Let's assume that this has dynamically provisioned a persistent volume and the associated storage.
Now this persistent volume claim is bounded to the persistent volume over here.
Now after a month a user has deleted the persistent volume claim.
Now the question that comes is what happens to this specific persistent volume?
Should it be deleted or in a production environment you might want to retain it.
Specifically, if it is a persistent volume for a pod like database.
So depending upon the type of use case, you have options on what happens to the persistent volume.
And that option can be configured using the reclaim policy.
So at an overview there are two primary reclaim policies that are available.
One is delete.
Second is retain.
Delete is very straightforward, which states that whenever a persistent volume claim is deleted, the
associated persistent volume will also be removed.
This is the simplest one.
Retain is also simple.
What?
It states that whenever a PVC is deleted, the persistent volume is not removed.
It continue to exist.
Alright, so the underlying storage and its data is preserved when you have this specific access mode.
Now when we discuss about the reclaim policy, it can be set specifically whenever you are creating
a persistent volume, or it can also be set at a storage class level.
Now, within your note that when you discuss about the reclaim policy setting at a persistent volume,
this is generally done when you have statically provisioning the persistent volume over here.
So you have a option of persistent volume reclaim policy.
Within here you can have the appropriate reclaim policy.
And then much more appropriate.
Specifically whenever you have a dynamic provisioning.
You can set it at a storage class level, where you have a reclaim policy and you can set to the appropriate
one.

--- Access Modes for PVC ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about the access mode specifically related to the persistent
volumes.
Now at a very high level overview, access mode defines how a specific persistent volume can be mounted
and accessed by a node and pods as part of your Kubernetes cluster.
Let's take an example where you have two worker nodes that are available, and in each worker node you
have a individual pod.
Now let's assume that there is a persistent volume that has been created.
Now this persistent volume can be mounted on a pod in a worker node one.
It can be mounted in a pod in a worker node two.
Now this is one possibility.
Second possibility is that this persistent volume can only be mounted in a single pod at a time.
So if this volume is mounted in port two, then you cannot mount it in pod one.
So there are multiple different type of approaches that are available.
Each one can be set using the access modes.
Now, in total there are four primary access modes that are available.
You have read, write.
Once you have read only many, you have read, write many and you have read write.
Once bought at a high level overview.
You should know what this means and also on how you can set these access modes.
Now the first one is the read write ones before we explore this.
One point to note is that you can set it as part of the persistent volume claim.
So in the PVC where you are requesting for a persistent volume in the access modes, you can set the
appropriate access mode.
Now as part of this slide, we are exploring the read write ones at an overview.
When you have this access mode, the volume can be mounted by a single node at a time.
Now when we discuss about the single node, it can also include multiple pods as part of the node.
So even if multiple pods are running on the same node, they can use the same PVC and mount the appropriate
persistent volume as part of the pod, and can perform the read and write operations to that specific
volume.
However, when you have pods that are running on a different node, they cannot simultaneously mount
this volume as a read write.
This is one point to note.
We will be discussing about this practically in just a moment.
However, just keep a note about how this allows the volume to be mounted by a single node at a time.
The second one is read only many.
Now in here you see access mode is read only many.
Now in this approach, the volume can be mounted as read only by many nodes simultaneously.
And this is the reason why multiple pods that are running in different worker nodes can mount and read
from this volume concurrently.
However, no pods will be able to write it.
This is the second mode.
The third mode is read write many.
In this approach, the volume can be mounted as read.
Write by many nodes simultaneously, and multiple pods that are running in different worker nodes can
mount these volumes and perform the read as well as write operations concurrently.
Now also note that although we are discussing about all of these access modes, the storage backend
should also support these shared access.
In case if it does not support, then you will not be able to use these modes.
And the fourth mode here is the read write once.
In this approach, the volume can be mounted as read write by a single pod only.
So this is one of the most restrictive mode.
Even if you have multiple ports as part of a single worker node, this volume at a time can be mounted
as read write by a single pod.
So this is the high level overview about the four important access modes.

--- Overview of ConfigMaps ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about an important topic of config maps.
Now generally in a Kubernetes cluster, one of the common objects that you will see running is a pod.
And generally what runs inside a pod, it is some form of application.
Now when there is an application that is running inside a pod, it needs to store some data.
So where will that data get stored?
In most of the cases, the data gets stored as part of an external database.
So when an application inside a pod wants to store some data to the database, it will also need the
information related to the database like the database user password, the database URL, etc..
Now, for such use cases, one of the common patterns that has been observed is that organizations will
hardcode the database credentials as part of the container image from which the pod got launched.
For example, let's consider you have a app pod.
Now the container image from which the pod was launched will have certain hard coded data like the DB
user, the db password, the db URL, so that once the application inside the port starts to run, it
can use these credentials to connect to the appropriate database, and maybe it can fetch the data,
it can store some data, and so on.
Now this kind of approach is also sometimes seen in many of the organizations.
The problem with this approach is that in case if certain aspects of this hard coded data needs to change,
for example, DB user has been changed or the database password has been changed after one year.
Now the problem is that since it is a hard coded data as part of a container image and you will have
to modify some part of the data, then essentially you will have to recreate a container image based
on a newer hard coded data.
And from the new container image you will have to recreate the pod as well.
And this kind of approach is generally not recommended in production setup.
So in order to overcome this you have a specific feature in Kubernetes called as config maps.
Config maps at a high level.
Overview.
It allows you to store key value pairs in a central manner.
So what you do?
You create a config map in your Kubernetes cluster.
So here you have two sets of config maps.
1st May be for each environment like dev environment, prod environment, etc..
And now what will happen is let's say you have a app pod that is launched in a production environment.
Then it can fetch from a broad based config map.
In a similar way, if you have a app pod that gets launched in a development environment, then it can
fetch the data from a development config map.
Now the benefit here is that there is no hard coding that is required as part of the container image,
nor you have to pass this data as part of the environment in pod manifest file.
Along with that, the next advantage is that this data, if it needs to change, you can directly modify
the config map with the updated Dbpassword and that's about it.
You will fetch the latest details from the pod.
All right.
So this is the basic of config map.
Let's go ahead and look into it from a demo perspective so that our concept is clear.
So currently from the CLI if I quickly do a cube CTL get config map.
You see I have certain config maps that are available.
This is the primary config map that we are looking into which is dev hyphen config.
Now if you explore this specific config map I will say kubectl describe config map of dev hyphen config.
You see this config map has certain data.

with the output of YAML.
So this time under the data you see you have certain data like db host Dbpassword db user.
Very similar to the diagram that you are seeing.
So this is the basic of config map.
As we are discussing, it allows you to basically store certain key value pairs that your application
can use.
Now, once you have a central config map that is available, the next important part is related to Pod.
Because Pod also needs to access the config map for a wide variety of use cases.
So for this I also have one pod that is available.
So when I do kubectl get pods, you see I have a test pod that is running.
And now we are going to connect to this pod to see on how config map data is available here.

feature in Kubernetes tries to solve.
Now before we conclude this video, certain pointers that you have to keep a note of.
First one is that the primary purpose of Configmap is to store non-sensitive configuration data that
application might need.
Why?
Because whatever data that you store as part of Configmap is generally stored in plain text.
And this is not intended for the sensitive information.

--- Practical 2 - ConfigMaps (Mounting to Pods) ---

Hi everyone, and welcome to the part two of the Configmap practical.

that is running inside the pod can use the data that is part of a specific configmap.
So this is the main area to learn as part of today's video.
Now in Kubernetes, there are multiple approaches that you can use in which the data from Configmap
can be used by the application inside a pod.
Two of the very common methods that are being used in organizations are through the environment variable
and through the volume mounts.
Generally, when you have a lot of data as part of configmap, volume mounts is one of the common approaches
that is being used.
So let's in fact, we'll go ahead and explore both of these methods.
The approach number one as we are discussing is related to volume mount.
What happens in this case is that the data that is part of a config map is mounted inside a pod as a
volume.
So in such cases, each key value pair that is part of config map appears as a file in the volume.
So in case if you have 40 to 50 key value pairs, then all of them will be added as part of the volume
that you mount inside the pod.

--- Security Context ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about security context.
Now before we do that, it is important for us to understand the challenge related to security pose,
which will be looking into how this specific feature helps.
So many times it is observed that whatever container that runs on a specific host system, these containers
run with root user privileges.
And this is very common for a wide range of organizations.
Now, although from the functionality point of view this is beneficial, but from the security point
of view it unnecessarily increases the attack surfaces.
For example, in case whenever you have some kind of a container breakout and the container is compromised,
then the attacker may be through.
Vulnerabilities can connect to the host system because ultimately the container is running on top of
host system.
If an attacker through the container manages to connect to the host system and their associated file,
then they can target a wide range of other devices.
Maybe there are other important production level containers that are running in the host system so they
can target them.
They can monitor the network traffic that is flowing between the containers, between client and the
containers and so on.
So one of the areas that makes the container breakout related attacks much more powerful is when the
container is running with the root user privilege.
So let's take a simple example that allows us to demonstrate the basic concept.
So for today's video I have a very simple port call an insecure port that is running.
It is based on BusyBox and you have a sleep command that is running.
Now what you are doing is we are mounting the root volume over here.
So this is the root and we are mounting it inside the container.
So ultimately all of the host files that are part of the host system will be available inside the container.
So let's go ahead and quickly do a kubectl apply on this specific YAML file.
Now once you have done that when you do a kubectl get pods we have a insecure port that is running.
Now let's quickly connect to this insecure pod.
Now, one of the issue that you will see over here is that when I run a ID command, you see the user
that we are logged in inside this specific container is the root user.
Now the problem with this approach is that in the host system.
So basically in here these are all of the directories that are part of the host system that are being
mounted inside the container.
Now this directory also contains a lot of important files like kernel, your Grub configuration etc..
So for example let's say you go to boot.
So within here you have your grub.
Again we are just taking a simple example.
Ideally you should not try and take example of Grub related configuration.
It can mess up the system.
But anyways, the thing that I wanted to show you, if you look into the permissions specifically related
to grub.cfg, you see you have a root and root, so only root user will be able to perform the right
operation on this specific file.
For example, if you go to Grub.cfg and then let's try to modify this file.
Anyways, it is clearly written do not edit this file, but we'll try to modify this file and we'll
save the change.
And you see we were able to successfully do that.
So if I quickly do a cat on grub.cfg you see our changes are getting reflected.
So in such cases if there is a container breakout that happens and the container is using a root level
privilege, then essentially the attacker will be able to connect to the host system.
He can load some malicious kernel modules and monitor the traffic and other activities.
So this is the reason why generally it is recommended that if not required, you should avoid running
the container with the root user privilege.
So in order to overcome these issues, one of the Of the recommendation is to go ahead and run the container
with a non-root privilege.
In such cases, what will happen is even if situations like container breakout happens and the attacker
tries to connect to critical host files, the access will be denied.
So overall, there will be a limited access to the host system in such kind of a scenario.
Now the question that comes is how can you specify what is the user that the container will run through.
And this is where the security context comes into picture.
At a high level overview security context, it defines the privilege and access control settings for
a pod or a container.
Now similar example.
However in the pod spec here you see you have a security context.
You have run as user 1000, run as group 1000.
So this specific container will not run with the root user privilege.
Alright, so as much as possible it is recommended that you use a non privileged user in production
environment.
Now when we discuss about security context, there are three important fields that we should be aware
of.
One is run as user, so you can specify the UID of a container process to run run as group.
Again this is the group ID and you have a FS group which is the group ID for the volume mounted files.
