--- Overview of Kubernetes Secrets ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about Kubernetes secrets.
Now one of the common issues that you will see in terms of security for many of the organizations is
that the container image from which Pod gets launched, if the application inside that container wants
to connect to some external system, it can be a database, it can be other websites.
Also, you will see that these containers often contain sensitive data that are hardcoded inside it,
like for example, passwords, tokens, etc..
So let's assume that you have a app pod over here, and this app pod wants to connect to a external
database.
Now from what is observed in many of the occasion is that in order for this connection to happen, the
app pod will also need certain important information like the database, user, database, passwords,
etc. and these credentials are generally hardcoded as part of the container image.
So whenever a pod gets launched from a container image, since the details are already there as part
of the image, the application inside the pod can use that to connect to the external system over here.
Now, from this specific diagram itself, you can identify what are the security related issues.
One of the common one is that since hard coding is done, not only you have to protect the port, but
you have to actually protect the Docker file based on which the container image is created.
Then you have to protect the container image by itself because it contains the sensitive information.
And then you have to protect the port by itself.
So this kind of an approach is a big no no from production perspective.
So in such cases where we say that hard coding should be avoided.
What is the alternative that Kubernetes offers.
And this is where the secrets feature comes into picture.
So at a high level overview, Kubernetes Secrets is a feature that allows us to store the sensitive
data.
So it is like a centralized store of all of the sensitive data that you might have and your application
will require.
For example, you have a centralized storage like this.
And within here you can store multiple set of sensitive information like database credentials, tokens,
passwords, etc..
And now whenever an application pod gets launched.
This pod can go ahead and mount these secrets inside it and can access the data accordingly.
Now, in case if you are familiar with the concepts of config map, this is very similar to the config
map in Kubernetes.
The only primary difference here is that this is specifically for storing of sensitive data.
Config map is for the storage of non sensitive information.
So let's do one thing.
Let's go ahead and understand this from a demo perspective.
And we'll have a separate practical video where we will be discussing about these things in detail.
Now from the terminal if I do a cube CTL get secret.
You see I have one secret that is currently available.
And when you do a cube CTL describe secret followed by this specific secret name within the data.
Over here you see you have a password which is ten bytes.
You have a username which is five bytes.
So just from the describe command it does not really show you the plaintext data associated with a specific
secret.
So now when you do a cube CTL get secret will specify the name of secret along with the output of YAML.
And now in the data you have this password and you have this username.
So this is one part.
Now next part that we were discussing is that once you have secret stored centrally and application
part, now you are not really hardcoding it.
So you really require that the secret be available inside the application part so that when application
starts, it can use this secret for the overall initialization to take place.
So in one more tab I'll quickly do a cube CTL get pods.
I have one pod running for today's demo.
Let's go ahead and quickly connect to this specific pod over here.
All right.
Now before we explore this in one more tab, if you'll quickly do a cube CTL describe pod followed by
the name of the pod you see in this specific pod, there is a secret volume that is mounted.
And what is the secret name?
The secret name is Secret basic a code which is this specific one.
So this specific secret is mounted inside the pod over here.
Now inside the pod when I go to etc. secret volume over here.
If I do a LRS, you see you have a password, you have a username.
And when I do a cat on username you will get a plaintext data.
In this case the username is admin and same for the password.
You can get it using the cat command.
Now before we conclude few pointers that you have to keep a note of specifically related to secrets.
Now in Kubernetes secrets by default configuration are not very secure.
Why?
Because generally when you create a new secret in Kubernetes in the data store associated with Kubernetes,
for example, in the etcd, these secrets are stored in plain text.
So here the encryption is not really applied by default.
However, at a later stage, in case if you'd like, you can go ahead and apply it.
So this facility is available along with adding the encryption.
You can also additionally protect the access to the secrets using Rbac.
So you don't really want all of the users in your Kubernetes cluster to connect to the secret.
So using Rbac, you can say that only a specific user or only a specific pod can go ahead and connect
to the secret to fetch the appropriate data.
All right.
So for this specific pointer, when we say secrets are not very secure, this is by default.
However, it is not that you cannot change it.
You can change it.
But this is like a default configuration.
Now the next important pointer that you need to keep a note is that whenever you view a secret, for
example, you use a kubectl get secret command.
You get the secret here, which is DB passes a key and this is the value.
So this is not a direct plaintext value.
This in fact is a base64 encoded format.
So in case if you want to view the actual value, you will have to use some external base64 decoder
to decode the secret fully.
Let's also explore this now.
For example, if you would notice when we did a cat on username, we got admin over here and when we
do a cat on password, we got a password called as Top secret.
However, when we ran this specific command over here, username is something like this password is
something like this.
So this is what we were referring to where this value that you get over here it is base64 encoded.
However, when a secret is mounted inside the pod, that is when the decode function will happen and
you will get the plaintext data.
Now let's also look into the decode here.
So you can just copy this just for an example.
And in Google when you type base64 decoder.
Now again note that sensitive data you should not really paste here, since this is a simple demo,
we are using that.
Ideally in Linux or Mac OS you have a base64 decode utility.
You can use that.
So within here you can just decode it.
And you see you got the top secret over here.
Great.
So I hope with this at a high level overview, you understood the basics of the Kubernetes Secrets functionality.
In the upcoming video, we will be exploring it from the practical point of view.

--- Practical - Kubernetes Secrets ---

Hi everyone, and welcome to the practical video associated with Kubernetes Secrets.

Now when we discuss about the overall practical, there are two important parts.
First part is you have to go ahead and learn on how you can create a Kubernetes secret.
As we know in Kubernetes Secret, you can have multiple set of secrets and each secret can have different
kind of data.

Now the next important component that we are going to discuss is the Cubelet.
Cubelet is generally part of the worker node, and the primary aim here is to be a node agent.
It interfaces with the container runtime to actually start the container.
Let us explore the process over here.
So whenever you create a new pod through kubectl, we know the request first goes to the API server.
Now from the API server again based on what scheduler.
Because scheduler will assign the appropriate worker node.
Once the node is assigned, the API server will send a request to the Kubelet associated with that worker
node to create a new pod.
Now Kubelet will interact with the underlying runtime.
It can be Containerd and various others.
And using this, a new container gets created as part of the worker node.
So Kubelet plays a very important role.
In case if Kubelet stops working, then the new pods will not really be created in that specific worker

--- Overview of Certificate Authority ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to quickly revise about the certificate authority, because this is
one of the first things that we will be setting up.
And for all of the Kubernetes components through the certificate authority will be signing the certificates.
So before we do that, I want to make sure that this concept is understood to avoid any confusion at
a later stage.
Now, at this stage, we know that when we want to configure a Kubernetes cluster, it is not just one
component.
There are multiple set of components that are involved.
So when you have multiple set of components, there will also be communication across these components.
And we want the communications to be secured.
This is the first point.
The second point is that the components also need a mechanism to verify each other's identity.
For example, if a kubelet that is running in a worker node sends some request to the API server, how
will kube API server verify the identity of the kubelet?
This is very important.
It can happen that the attacker is trying to send a request to the kube API server, saying that he
is the Kubelet.
So should the kube API server send the details to the attacker.
Answer is no.
So in order to achieve a proper solution for the use case one and this specific use case certificates
are used.
Now when we discuss about certificates.
Certificate authority is one of the first things that needs to be configured.
Ultimately, certificate authority is an entity that issues the digital certificates.
So here what will happen.
First, the certificate authority will have its own certificate and its own key.
And then this certificate authority will issue signed certificate for various components.
For example the certificate authority will issue the certificate for the API server for the scheduler,
the controller manager, Cubelet, cube, proxy, etc. and this specific certificate authority will
be trusted by both the receiver and the sender.
So this way what happens is let's assume that kube API server is the receiver and Cubelet is the sender.
Now kube API server will verify whether the certificate that has been presented by the Cubelet is issued
by this trusted certificate, authority or not.
If it is issued by the trusted certificate authority.
The kube API server will assume that the entity is what it claims to be, and the communication will
happen successfully.
So let's also quickly look into high level overview on how exactly this might look like.
Now for today's demo I have a certificate authority certificate.
So you have one certificate authority certificate and the second certificate authority certificate.
Now when you have the certificate authority using this certificate authority you can issue signed certificates
for other entities.
So let's also quickly look into it.
Now again note that this is a demo video.
You can just understand it conceptually.
So here what we are doing is we are creating a certificate for the name of Zalora.
Now this certificate that is created, if you see this is the certificate of zeal.
Zeal.
And this is the key similar to this, the certificate authority will also issue certificate for the
kube API, server for the controller manager, etc..
Now you can verify whether this zeal certificate that I am presenting to a website.
Is it signed by the trusted certificate authority or not?
So let's assume that a website trusts this certificate.
So what happens is website says that any certificate that has been signed by this specific CA, I will
trust it.
So there is a way in which you can do a verification.
So you have open SSL, verify you are using the example org certificate authority certificate and then
you say Zeel dot cert.
So if I press enter you see it says okay.
That means that Zeel dot cert has been issued by this trusted CA.
Now I also have one more certificate authority of Kubernetes.
Now if I try to use the Kubernetes certificate authority let's verify.
At this stage it shows error loading file.
So let's do one thing.
Let's just copy this.
Let's do an LSE.
Let's run this command once again.
Let's make sure there are no typos.
Now when I press enter you see it says Is verification field.
So this means that this certificate authority certificate was not used to sign this specific certificate
of zeal.
And this is where the second part comes into picture, which states that the key part is both the receiver
and the sender trusts the CA.
So if this specific CA is signing the certificate for all of the components here, all of the components
must also say that I trust this CA.
So I trust all of the components that has the signed certificate from the trusted CA.
All right.
So this is one part to note.
Now when we go ahead and configure Kubernetes cluster from scratch.
First thing that we will be doing is we will be creating the certificate authority certificate.

--- Kubelet Preferred Address Type - New ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.

Now, one thing that needs to be noted is that when we run commands like kubectl exec, when you want
to connect to the container, kube API server will receive the request and it will initiate the connection
with the kubelet that is running on the host.
As we know, each host runs a kubelet.
So for example, you have the API server over here API server.
In order to connect to the Kubelet, it will use certain information like either the host name or the
IP address, etc..
So let's assume that the API server uses the host name to connect to the Kubelet.
But if the host name is not resolvable, then the API server will not be able to communicate to the
Kubelet.
So this is the reason why it is important for us to know that in scenarios where the host names of the
worker nodes are not resolvable, we also can connect using the IP address.
Let's also explore this now.
At this stage when I do kubectl get pods, there are certain pods running.
Now when I do kubectl exec on any of the pod, let's say nginx pod.
This is working.
Why this is working?
Because we have a entry in the etc. host.
This is the entry that is resolving this worker to the IP address.
So API server knows that this worker is running on this IP address and the kubectl exec works.
But as soon as we remove the entry on the etc. hosts over here.
And now.
When you try to connect you see we are getting error related to resolution.
So ideally what you would like is when you do a kubectl get nodes, you have a worker node.
And when you do a kubectl describe node say worker.
Now if you go a bit up there are two important information here in the addresses.
You have the internal IP and you have the host name.
So by default the API server tries to connect to the kubelet using the host name.
In this case it is worker since it is not resolvable if we do not add it as part of the etc. host entry,
you get an error.
So what you can say to the cube API server is that instead of trying to connect to the Cubelet using
the host name, use the internal IP over here.
This is the IP address.
If IP address is presented to you, no name resolution is required, so this can work perfectly well.
So this specific configuration can be achieved using the Kubelet preferred address type.
Now if you go ahead and open the lecture associated with the Kubelet preferred address type within here.
Initially we have documented steps like from the host entry, remove this and try to connect.

We'll clear the screen.

--- Overview of Network Policies ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
Today we are going to go ahead and discuss about an interesting topic of network policies.
Now in case if you have worked with firewalls it can be a software based firewalls like iptables.
Or it can be a cloud specific firewall offerings like for example in AWS you have security group, you
have network ACLs, etc. irrespective of that, if you have worked with firewalls, then this topic
of network policies will be easier for you to understand at a high level.
Overview.
Network policies provides similar feature to that of firewall, but is specific for ports.
Now, one very important point that needs to be noted is that in a Kubernetes cluster, whenever you
launch multiple set of pods, these pods will be able to communicate with each other by default.
So Kubernetes allows the pods to communicate with each other in the cluster.
And there are no restrictions in these set of communications.
So for example pod one can connect to pod two.
It can also connect to port.
Three.
And similarly, all of the ports will be able to inter communicate with each other.
Now at an overview this is fine, but in a longer term when you have a production related setup, this
is something that you do not really want.
So let's understand this with a challenge.
So let's assume that one of the ports that is part of your Kubernetes cluster is compromised.
So some application that was running in this port and that application is compromised and the attacker
has access to it.
Now what attacker can do since by default this compromised port can communicate with all other ports
that are part of the Kubernetes cluster.
Attacker can use this port one to attack all other ports that are part of the cluster.
And this is something that you do not really want.
This unnecessarily increases the attack surface area and gives attacker a better chance to compromise
other ports as well.
So in an ideal scenario, what you would like Is that only the pot that have genuine requirement to
connect to other ports?
These connections should be allowed.
Rest.
All of the connections should be blocked.
For example, application port will require to connect to the database port, so this connection should
be allowed.
But there is also a test port that is running.
You do not really want test port to connect to the database port and fetch all of the important data.
So this kind of communication should not be allowed and it should be blocked.
So this specific part on what communication should be allowed between ports, what communication should
not be allowed, etc..
This part can be achieved using network policies.
So at a very high level.
Overview.
Network policies are mechanism for controlling the network traffic flow in a Kubernetes cluster.
For example, let's assume that these are the three ports that are part of the cluster.
Now you can go ahead and create network policies and associate it to the their respective port.
So if you look into the network policy here, it states.
Sources app port destination is database port effect is allowed.
So now what will happen?
Any communication between app port and the database port here.
Will be allowed.
Similarly you have a source of test port destination is all effect is denied.
So test port will not be able to communicate with any other entity like ports as part of the.
Kubernetes cluster.
And using this network policies you can go ahead and design the idle network communication.
Based scenario for your Kubernetes cluster.
Now when we discuss about network policies and in fact when you also discuss about any firewalls, you
will typically create two set of rules.
One is the ingress rule also referred to as a inbound rule.
Second, you refer to it as a egress rule or an outbound rule.
So just for an example, let's say that you have a Enginex pod over here.
Now if a server or if a pod wants to communicate to the nginx pod.
So this is an incoming connection and is referred to as ingress.
Similarly, nginx pod might want to communicate with other pod or nginx pod might want to communicate
with the internet.
So this part of communication from this nginx pod towards another entity, this is referred to as a
egress connection.
So whenever you create network policies, you can set the rules at a ingress level or at a egress level
as well.
And you can combine them as well based on the requirement.
So let us also take an example with respect to firewall inside DigitalOcean.
So whenever you create a firewall you specify the inbound rules over here.
And you specify the outbound rules over here.
Similar to this when we discuss about network policies, also you specify the inbound rule and you specify
the outbound rule.
The primary difference here is that this firewall that you create in, say, DigitalOcean, this can
connect to a server.
However, this specific rules that we create, these are primarily associated with pods.
Now that we understand the basics, let's go ahead and take a step further to understand things in more
detail.
So let's assume that you have a source port over here and you want to set up a network policy.
So whenever you create a network policy, this policy has certain identifiers that it can use as part
of the filter.
For example this policy can be based on other ports.
It can be based on namespaces.
It can also be based on IP blocks.
All right.
So you have the port selector the namespace selector and the IP block.
These are the three very important entities based on which you can filter the incoming as well as the
outgoing connection from a specific source port.
So let's take one example of each one of them, and will also have a demo that will allow us to ensure
that our base concept is clear.
Now the first example is related to the port selector.
So what it states allow ports with a label of role equals to app, which is this one to connect to port
with a label of role equals to database.
So now what will happen.
Any port which has a role equals to app will be able to communicate to a port which has role equals
to database.
This as we were discussing this is like a genuine connection because application will have to connect
to the database.
And then what will happen in other cases is that any other port that does not have this label of role
equals to App when it tries to connect to a port with a role equals to database, that connection will
be denied.
Alright, let's have a quick demo so that we understand this topic in better terms.
Now for today's demo I have a network policy that is created.
The name of the network policy is Pod Selector.
Now I'll also do a kubectl get pods which show labels.
And currently we have three pods that are running.
Each pod has certain set of labels.
So now let's do one thing.
Let's do a kubectl describe network policy of pod selector.
And let's try to read what exactly it states.
So this is the area that we are focusing.
So first one is the pod selector which is role equals to database.
Now this part.
Now again there are two pod selector here.

--- Scheduling Pods without a Scheduler ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
Now in today's video, we will be discussing about static pots.
Now, we already know that a scheduler is responsible for scheduling a pod on a given worker node.
So when you do a cube, Ctl run, which basically creates a deployment, then where will your pod be
assigned?
Because there can be hundreds of worker nodes.
So decision on where a pod can run is decided by the scheduler.
Now, once a node is decided by the scheduler, your API server communicates with the Cubelet, and
Cubelet in turn takes care of running the pod.
We have already seen this specific architecture in the section one.
So you have a cube scheduler, you have a cube API server.
The cube scheduler here is responsible for scheduling a pod on a given worker node and your cube API
server.
It connects with the kubelet of various worker nodes and it can inform the Cubelet that you need to
run a specific pod.
So this is the basic architecture that we already know.
Now your cubelet basically it takes the information from the API server related to the pod specification
and it creates the pod accordingly.
So it is not necessary for Cubelet to always make use of the instructions from the cube API server.
So let's say that this specific left side component is not present at all.
So the connectivity between the Cubelet and your cube API server is not present due to some reason.
So that is the scenario here and you want to schedule a pod on this specific worker node.
All right.
So now what you can do is you can directly tell that cubelet that hey, can you run a specific pod?
So Cubelet will take your instruction which you have told to the cubelet directly without the cube API
server and Cubelet will take that instruction and it will run that pod.
All right.
So that specific aspect is also referred as a static pod.
So let's do one thing.

dot directory specifically related to startups.

--- Taints and Tolerations ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
Now in today's video we are going to discuss about an interesting topic of taints and tolerations.
So let's get started.
So at a high level overview, when we discuss about taint taint, whenever it is added to a Kubernetes
node, it allows us to repel certain pods from that specific node.
Let's understand this with an example where you have a worker node one, you have a worker node two
and you have a pod one.
Now this pod one needs to be scheduled.

--- Capacity, Allocated, and Allocatable ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to go ahead and discuss about the capacity allocable and allocated as
part of the appropriate Kubernetes nodes.
Now, whenever you go ahead and run a command of kubectl describe node followed by the node name, you
will get a detailed information about the node.
It will show you about the node capacity, the allocable resources, how much resources are allocated,
and various other information.
So in today's video, it is important for us to understand certain sections, specifically the capacity
allocable and allocated.
Before we go ahead and look into each one of them, let's see on where do we find this.
Now from the terminal, when you run a command say kubectl get nodes, it will show you the nodes related
information.
So let's say when I do kubectl describe node followed by the name of the node.
As we see here, we get a lot of information about the appropriate node.
Among this we are interested in few areas here.
The first important area here is the capacity.
Second important area here is this table.
And the third important area here is the allocated.
So let's go ahead and understand what each one of these means.
The first important area is the capacity.
And at a high level overview.
This represents the total amount of resources that is physically available on the node hardware itself.
So here it is showing you the CPU the ephemeral storage, the memory.
So CPU and memory is something that we have to be very thorough with in terms of understanding.
So CPU is showing as one what it means.
It means that the node has one CPU core or a virtual core.
Then you have the memory.
So this is the memory.
So this means around 1.92 Gib of total memory that is available.
Now again you will have to do the appropriate conversion.
And then you have the ephemeral storage.
Again you'll have to do slight conversion, so at this stage it converts to around 49 GB of local ephemeral
storage over here.
So this is related to the capacity.
The second important area is the alloc table.
Now this section shows the resources that are available for pods.
Now one thing to note is that let's assume that the node has around 1.92 GB of Ram and one core CPU.
Now each node only running the pods and there is no nodes might also be running other services to keep
the node running.
So those services will also require certain amount of memory and certain amount of CPU.
So out of this, 100% of CPU and 100% of memory cannot be allocated to the pods because ultimately maybe
you might have Docker, you might have container D, you will have the kube proxy, you will have the
kubelet that might be responsible for creating and managing the containers.
So all of those will also be using the CPU and memory.
So this is the reason why generally whenever you create a pod and when you set a the request and limits,
you cannot directly rely just on the capacity to write the appropriate requests and limits.
So this is where the alloc table can also prove to be useful.
At a high level overview, this section shows the resources that are available for ports.
After subtracting what the system which can be the operating system, the kubelet, etc. reserves.

--- Container Runtime Interface (CRI) ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to go ahead and discuss about the container runtime interface.
Now one point that we have to keep a note of is that in the earlier stage of developments, Kubernetes
had a tight coupling with Docker, and this was directly integrated as part of the Kubelet code as well.
So in the earlier versions of Kubernetes, the Kubelet interacted with the containers primarily through
the Docker engine over here.
So this is one point that we have to keep a note of.
Now, as the time progressed and the container ecosystem evolved, there were new runtimes that were
emerging.
Like container you have Cri-o, you have Mirantis, etc. and when you have new container runtimes that
were emerging to support them, Kubernetes introduced the container runtime interface as part of the
Kubernetes.
And now you will see that there are multiple popular CRI compatible container runtimes that are available.
You have Containerd, you have Cri-o, you have Docker Engine that is supported through CRI Docker.
D you also have Mirantis, container runtime and so on.
Now note that at a later stage when you had the container runtime interface, this specific tight coupling
with the Docker was removed and organizations had much more better flexibility on what type of container
runtime they want to use in the environment.
Now discussing about the container runtime interface.
At a very high level overview, you can consider it to be like a plugin interface or an API that allows
the Kubelet to communicate with various container runtimes.
For example, let's assume that you have a worker node, and in the worker node you have the Kubelet.
Now this Kubelet through the container runtime interface, it can connect to the appropriate container
runtime, and it is the container runtime that is responsible for creating and managing the containers.
Now, as we are discussing in the earlier version of Kubernetes, there was a very tight coupling between
a Kubelet and Docker, and this was also as part of the Kubelet code.
And this tight coupling created a lot of issues specifically related to the newer runtimes that organizations
might wanted to use.
And this is the reason why, to keep things much more flexible, you have the container runtime interface
and any container runtime that supports the container runtime interface.
The Kubelet will be able to connect to the appropriate container runtime, and the containers can be
created and managed accordingly.
Now, one more thing that we have to keep a note of is that container runtime is one of the foundational
softwares that allows the containers to operate on the host system, and it is the container runtime
that is responsible for various important tasks like pulling the container images, managing the container
lifecycle, and running the container on the host system.
So container runtime is extremely important.
Now ultimately what Kubelet will do is it receives the instruction from the kube API server and whatever
instruction it receives, like a new port needs to be created.
This instructions will be passed on to the appropriate container runtime, stating that new containers
from this image needs to be created, and it is the container runtime which creates the appropriate
containers.
Now, when you look into the documentation associated with the container runtime interface, let's look
into it.
It states that the CRI is a plugin interface, which enables the Kubelet to use a wide variety of container
runtimes without having a need to recompile the cluster components.
Something similar to what we saw in the first slide, where there was a direct integration of Dockershim
in the Kubelet code.
So this is something that needs to be avoided because there are a wide variety of container runtimes
for each container runtime.
You don't really want a hard integration, and this is the reason why the container runtime interface
proves to be very important.
Note that this is not like a software component, it is the way in which the Kubelet connects to the
appropriate container runtime.
Now the second point also states that you need a working container runtime on each node in your cluster,
so that the Kubelet can launch the pod and their containers.
So the Kubelet is not responsible for creating the The containers.
It is the container runtime that is responsible for that.
And the third point is very important, which states that the container runtime interface is the main
protocol for the communication between the Kubelet and the container runtime.
Something similar to what you see over here.
And the fourth point states that the container runtime interface in turn defines the main gRPC protocol
for the communication between the node components, which are the Kubelet and the container runtime.
So using this, the Kubelet connects to the container runtime.
You have a common set of protocols which the Kubelet as well as the container runtime understands.
And this is how the communication happens.
Now discussing about the container runtime, let's go ahead and look into what are the options that
are available.
Now within your one point that we were discussing, even here, it is written that the Kubernetes releases
before version 1.24 included a direct integration with Docker Engine using a component named Docker
shim, and this direct integration has been removed and it is no longer part of the Kubernetes.
So this is one point that you have to keep a note of.
Now discussing about the container runtime, one more point to note is that the Kubernetes requires
that you use the container runtime that conforms to the container runtime interface.
This is very important, and there are multiple set of container runtimes that are available.
For example you have container D, you have Cri-o, you have Docker Engine using the CRI docker D,
and you also have the Mirantis container runtime.
Now if you go a bit down, these are some of the generic configurations that you might have to do,
but we are more interested in container runtime specific details.
So in the container runtime the first one is the container D.
And within here it is showing some of the important configurations related to each container runtime
like for example the default CRI socket and so on.
And similar configurations will be for Cri-o and Docker Engine and others.
Now, depending upon what container runtime you want to use, you can go ahead and look into the appropriate
instructions here.
Now, let me quickly give you an overview on how things might look like in a Kubernetes based cluster.
Now if you'll quickly do kubectl get nodes currently you see we have one node that is available and
the status is ready.
Now within here since this node for example when I do kubectl get pods, currently I have some pods
that are running.
Now we know that since the pods that are running, you must have a container runtime and you must also
have a kubelet.
So if I do systemctl status kubelet.
At this stage we have the Kubelet component that is available.
Now, in fact, let's quickly revise the cluster architecture.
Otherwise this will lead to confusion.
So generally you have some main components as part of the control plane like the API server, etcd scheduler,
controller manager, etc. and in each node you will have a Kubelet and you will have a kube proxy.
We are more interested in the Kubelet Kubelet as we know it connects to the appropriate container runtime
and containers are created.
So here you see you have a CRE container runtime interface.
So when the kube API server sends a message to the Kubelet stating that you need to run one pod based

So kubelet, once it receives the instruction from the kube API server, it will pass it on to the appropriate

--- Configuring cri-docker ---

Hi everyone and welcome back.
In today's video, we are going to discuss about the configuration related to the CRI docker d.
Now at an overview, the cri docker d is primarily like an adapter that implements the Kubernetes container
runtime interface for Docker.
Now, earlier the shim was as part of the Kubelet, so the code was integrated within the Kubelet and
the Kubelet was able to directly communicate with the Docker engine.
However, at a later stage to support multiple container runtimes, this hard coding of the code as
part of the Kubelet was removed, and in this case, if you wanted the Kubelet and the Docker engine
communication to work, you can go ahead and make use of the CRI dockerd, which will act as an adapter
for that.
So in this case, the Docker engine will be responsible for creating and managing the containers in
your environment.
So at an overview it will translate the container runtime interface gRPC calls from Kubernetes into
the Docker API calls.
Now in today's video what we are going to do first in a server, we are going to set up the Docker Engine.
This Docker engine is responsible for creating and managing the containers.
Now Kubelet directly cannot interact with the Docker engine, so you will need one more component which
acts as a middleman, which is the CRI docker d.
So the kubelet will connect to the cri docker de cri de coeur d as we know it will translate the appropriate
cri gRPC calls from Kubernetes to the Docker API calls over here.
So let's go ahead and try it out.
Now the cri docker d is managed under mirantis.
So if you see you have the appropriate instruction what it states.
This adapter provides a shim for Docker engine that lets you control Docker via the Kubernetes container
runtime interface.
Now for today's practical, I have a fresh server based on ubuntu 24 LTS in this server.
First we are going to install the Docker engine.
We are going to use the cri docker d, and then we are going to set up the cube adm and will test the

--- Understanding Docker Logging Drivers ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
In today's video, we will be discussing about the Docker logging drivers.
Now, typically in a Linux or Unix subsystem, whenever you run a Unix and Linux command, they open
up three input output streams.
Now these are referred as standard input.
You have standard output and you have standard error.
And similar applies for the Docker containers that you are running.
So let's say you have running certain Docker containers.
Now these would have a standard input.
It will also have a standard output.
It will also have a standard error.
Now if you remember during the earlier videos where we were discussing about the importance of the IT
flag, now generally in Docker we specify the hyphen I and hyphen T flag so that your terminal basically
attaches to the standard input.
So standard input is where you would provide the input to this specific process or the command.
So you have a bash where you can specify some input like command or a CD command.
So that input can come from various sources like keyboard.
So that is what standard input is.
Now standard output is where, let's say let's take an example of Enginex now.
So Nginx can have a lot of access logs within its standard output.
So those access logs, so you have let's assume you have Nginx running on port 80 and 100 people are
connecting to your Nginx so those logs nginx can share it to the standard output.
You also have standard error where you have error related logs that can be present over here.
So Docker allows you to monitor the standard output as well as the standard error with the help of various
type of logging drivers.
Because many times it is important for you to see what is the standard output data, what is the standard
error data?
So those can be achieved with the help of logging driver.
So let's quickly understand this with a quick practical demo.
So I'm in my CLI if I quickly do a docker.
PS currently we do not have any container up and running, so let's quickly start a container.

which is constantly running is ping, google.com.
So this output of this specific command, which is running this output, it can share it to the standard
output.
So if you want to see a standard output or even a standard error associated with this specific container,
you can make use of the Docker logs command.
So you can see Docker logs.
My busy box.
And now you see, you are able to see the output of the command which is running, which is it is able
to get the reply associated with Google.com server.
So I hope at a high level overview you understood what the Docker logs command does.
Docker Logs command allows you to get the standard output as well as the standard error associated with
the container.
Now there are a lot of type of logging drivers because if you if you remember, if when we had pressed
the Docker logs.
So this should be stored in some kind of a file, let's say you might want to send it in a centralized
location.
So depending upon your requirement, you can make use of certain logging drivers which are available
in Docker.
So if you basically do a Docker info command within the log here, you see there are various type of
logging drivers.
You have logs, you have fluentd, you have GCP logs, you have journaled Json file, local Splunk syslog
and various others.
So these are the types of logging drivers which are available for the Docker.
Now, depending upon the requirement, let's say that you want to send all the logs for Docker.
Let's say you have something similar to the demo that we did.
We are doing a ping on google.com and you want to send all of those standard output logs to the AWS
Cloudwatch service.
So then you can make use of the logging driver of logs.
If you want to send it to a splunk instance, you can use the Splunk driver.
If you want to send it to syslog, you can use a syslog driver and various others.
Now typically if you quickly do a Docker info and let's grep on logging driver, you would see that
there will be one logging driver which is the default one.
So in this case the logging driver, which is the default one is Json hyphen file.
So anytime when you create a container and you do not specify a logging driver by default, Docker will
associate the Json hyphen file logging driver with your container so we can even find it out.
So if you do a Docker inspect on my BusyBox, let's do that and let's go a bit up.
So here you will see within the log config you have the type as Json hyphen file.
Now along with that, one important part to remember is because we are making use of the Docker logs
command.
Let's open this up.
So all of these data that you see over here, it gets stored in a file.
So in case if you want to see on which file all of the logs are being stored, you can do it with Docker
inspect.

a Docker log.
So all of these logs are being stored in this specific directory.
Now along with that, let's quickly do a Docker.
PS Let's assume that you want to create new container with a different logging driver.

So let's try it out.

It basically says that error response from daemon configured logging driver does not support reading.
So depending upon the logging driver that you choose, the amount of configuration which is required
would differ.
Now a few important details that you need to remember.
The first is that there are a lot of logging drivers which are available in Docker.
We have already seen now some of these logging driver includes you have Json file, you have none,
you have syslog, you have local, you have journaled Splunk logs and there are various others which

Now comes the important point that the Docker Logs command is not available for the drivers other than

Json file.
Now if you are using some custom driver like Splunk, like logs, et cetera, then the Docker logs will

So that's about it for the logging driver.
Now do remember that depending upon the logging driver that you choose, there can be certain caveats
that can happen.
So let's say you are choosing a syslog based logging driver and you have a centralized syslog server

So make sure that whichever logging driver that you implement for your environment understand about
the advantages as well as the disadvantages of those logging driver and then only implement them accordingly.
So this is the high level overview about the logging drivers which are available in Docker.

--- Monitoring Cluster Component Logs ---

Hey, everyone.
And welcome back.
Now, in today's video, we'll be discussing about the cluster component logs.
Now for every component within the cluster, be it a cube API server, the scheduler, the controller
manager, the Kubelet and others, all of them have the log files associated with them.
And whenever you are troubleshooting something logs becomes the primary factor based on which you can
identify the issue.
Now, if we are making use of a system, then you can look into the component level logs with the help
of the Journalctl command.
Now we have extensively made use of Journalctl while we were configuring our Kubernetes cluster from
scratch.
So I hope you understood what exactly this does.
Now within the official documentation over here, you will see that under the section of looking at
the logs, they have specified the log files associated with various components.
So for the master server components, you have log kube API server dot log.
So this is for the API server.

--- Pod Lifecycle Phases ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video at a high level overview, we are going to discuss about the basics of the pod lifecycle
phases.
Now, one point that we have to keep a note of is that in Kubernetes, the pods go through several lifecycle
phases from pod creation to the pod termination year.
So understanding at a high level overview about these phases is crucial.
Specifically when you are debugging and managing the workloads in the cluster.
Now when we discuss about these lifecycle phases it starts with pending.
Then you can have running.
Then you can have succeeded.
Then you can also have failed.
And you also have unknown.
So these are the five primary lifecycle phases that are available.
Let's go ahead and at a high level overview look into each one of them.
So one of the first phases here is the pending.
Pending generally can mean that the pod is accepted by Kubernetes.
But the containers are not yet created.
So generally the pod can be as part of the pending phase due to lot of reason.
One of the reason being the scheduling, then it can also be in pending when the Kubernetes is downloading
the appropriate container image.
Now, one point that we have to keep a note of is that Pod can also stay in the pending phase, if there
are any issues with the scheduling.
So let's say that there are ten worker nodes.
Now the Kubernetes is not able to determine the appropriate worker node for the pod based on the requirement
that you have set.
So in such cases, the pod will continue to stay in pending phase till the time the appropriate worker
node is available that satisfy the requirements of a pod.
The second common phase is running.
This means that the pod has been bound to an appropriate worker node, and all of the containers as
part of the pod have been created.
It can also mean that at least one of the containers is running, or is in the process of starting or
restarting.
So if you see in the status, you have two pods in running state over here, then you have the phase
of succeeded.
This means that all the containers in the pod have been terminated in success and will not be restarted.
Now we are going to discuss about this in just a moment in a practical point of view.
However, if you see in the status you have completed and this is the test board.
So maybe whatever application that was running or whatever script that you had defined as part of the
port, that script has been completed successfully and the port operation has been succeeded here.
Then you have the phase of field.
Again, this can occur due to multiple set of reasons.
Here you can consider in multiple scenarios that all the containers in the pods have been terminated,
and at least one container has terminated in failure here.
And then you have the phase of unknown.
So unknown is generally due to some reason the state of port could not be obtained.
Many a times it happens when there is an error in communication with the worker node, in which the
port should ideally be running.
Now, before we start with the practical, one more thing that we have to be aware of is related to
the port status field.
Now generally when you run kubectl get pods, you get the status field over here and in the status you
also get a message.
So at a high level overview, the status column in commands like kubectl get pods does not always directly
map to the five official pod lifecycle phases.
For example, here the status is pending and the phase is also pending.
So this is simple to understand.
Then you have a phase of running.
The status is also running.

The status is a little different.

It is not one of the five official phases that we just discussed.

status column output.

--- Container Restart Policy ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the container restart policy.
Again, this is an important topic.
And generally in production environments, the knowledge that you will gain as part of today's video
will prove to be useful.
So let's go ahead and discuss this in detail.
Now at a high level overview, you can consider that restart policies can provide self-healing feature
for containers.
Now if you look into the screenshot you have an app that is running.
The status is in error and there is a restart that is happening.
That is true.
So Kubernetes has the ability to restart the containers whenever specific issue occurs like an error.
So restart policies helps here.
And at an overview they specify the condition in which the container that is running inside a pod can
automatically be restarted.
So you don't really have to manually restart it.
Kubernetes based on the condition it will automatically restart the container as part of the pod.
Now, one very important point to note is that there are multiple set of restart policies that are available
in Kubernetes.
Based on the requirement, you can set each one of them accordingly.
One of the common one is always so.
When this restart policy is applied, it instructs Kubernetes to restart a container whenever it terminates,
regardless of whether the exit was due to success, which is exit code zero or failure.
And this is the default restart policy.
So even if you create a pod without any restart policy, always is the restart policy that will be used.
We'll be discussing about all of this practically in just a moment, but just let's quickly discuss
theoretically first.
The second restart policy is on failure.
In such cases, Kubernetes will only restart container if it terminates with non-zero exit code indicating
a failure.
This is slightly different from always in always, even if the container exit due to success with the
exit code of zero, it will still restart, and the third restart policy is never.
The name itself clearly states that Kubernetes should not restart the container, even if it exists
both at a success or a failure level.
Let's discuss about all of these restart policies.
From a practical point of view, this will give us better understanding.
Now, as part of today's practical, we are going to explore each restart policy in detail.
The first one that we are going to explore is the always restart policy.
As we were discussing, this is the default restart policy.
So whenever you create a pod for example through this command the always restart policy will apply over
here.
Now before we run this command I wanted to show you one thing.
So let's quickly create a pod.
Let's just call it as nginx pod from the image of nginx.
Now this is a simple command every one of us understands.
So now when you do kubectl get pods, you see at this stage we have nginx pod that is running.
The status is running.
And the restart at this stage is zero because nginx process is working perfectly well.
Now after clearing the screen, let's run the simple command of kubectl get pod nginx pod with the output
of YAML.
So basically we want to see what is the restart policy that got applied to this specific pod.
So let's go a bit up.
We are more interested in the spec section.
This is status section.
We are more interested in spec.
So in the spec just search for restart policy.
This is what we are interested in.
You see restart policy by default.
Even if we have not explicitly specified it is always so.
This is one important learning.
Now let's go ahead and understand the importance of the always restart policy.
So let's just copy this and we'll add it over here.
Now before we run it let's quickly explore what exactly this command does.
So it creates a new pod called as test pod from the image of BusyBox.
And here we are running a command called as non-existent command.
So this command as we know does not really exist.
For example, if you just run something like this, because this command does not really exist, you
will get an error.

So first there was restart count of zero.

--- Version Skew Policy ---

Hi everyone, and welcome back.
In today's video we are going to discuss about the version skew policy in Kubernetes.
Now, one point that we already know is that Kubernetes consists of multiple set of components behind
the scenes.
So when we discuss about control plane node there are multiple components like API server, controller,
manager, scheduler.
Then in worker node you have two important components like Kubelet kube proxy.
Now one point to note is that in Kubernetes it can happen that different components like API server
controller manager are interacting with each other across various versions.
So it can happen that kube API server for example is on version one.
Controller manager is in version 1.1.
Scheduler is in the version of 1.2.
Now, when you have different components with different version, the question is will your cluster
work perfectly well?
And the answer to that is it depends.
And primarily to deal with this issue where there can be multiple versions of components, you have
the version skew New policy that is made available to us.
Now, the main aim of this specific policy is to ensure that whatever component versions that are running
these versions should be compatible with each other and it should be stable.
So the version skew policy defines how versions of these components can differ while still maintaining
a functional cluster.
So you do not really want the controller manager to be version 1.1 and Apiserver to be 1.0, only to
realize that after a few months you are facing a lot of issues.
So to avoid all of these issues at a later stage, it is important for us to understand the version
skew policy.
Now, at a very high level overview version skew happens when two components that are interacting with
each other are not running at the exact same version.
For example, you have a kubectl on version 1.26 API server on version 1.33.
So this is a big difference in terms of version.
Now in Kubernetes it is not compulsory that all of the components needs to be on the exact same version.
Certain level of version skew is allowed.
However, whenever you have excessive difference between version, it can lead to compatibility issues,
failures, or unexpected behaviors.
So, for example, version 1.26 of kubectl might work with the API server, but it is not 100% guaranteed
that everything will work.
It can lead to compatibility issues that you will realize maybe after six months in production environments,
it can lead to certain failures or unexpected behaviors.
So this is the reason why understanding the version skew policy is important over here.
Now, before we explore the version skew policy, it is important for us to note on how the Kubernetes
versions are released.
So at a high level overview, Kubernetes versions are expressed as x dot y dot z where x is the major
version, y is the minor version, and z is the patch version.
So the format is major dot or minor dot patch.
Like 1.32.2.
Now that we understand the basics, let's look into the version skew policy for various components.
First important component is the cube API server.
And when we discuss about cube API server, you can have a single node running cube API server in production
environment.
Generally you can also have cube API server running in a highly available cluster based environment.
Now if you look into this specific architecture diagram, you have a load balancer and there are multiple
servers or multiple virtual machines where components of the control plane nodes are configured.
You have API server configured on multiple virtual machines, controller manager configured, scheduler
configured, etcd configured, and near the load balancing happens.
So in case even if one server goes down, you don't really need to worry, the load balancer can send
the request to the other working nodes.
Now that we understand it at a high level overview, the first pointer will make better sense, which
states that in a highly available based clusters, the newest and the oldest kube API server instance
must be within one minor version.
For example, if the newest cube API server is 1.32, then the other cube API servers that are supported
is either 1.32, which is the same version, or 1.31.
So this is one minor version difference.
Specifically, when we discuss about Ha based clusters.
Now the next important component is the Kubelet.
This is very important.
Kubelet must not be newer than the cube API server, and the second point states Kubelet may be up to
three minor version older than the cube API server.
So if the cube API server is 1.32, then 1.32 of Kubelet is supported, and then the three minor version
1.31, 1.30, and 1.29.
The next important component is the cube proxy.
Similar to Kubelet, you have to ensure that cube proxy must not be newer than the cube API server,
and it can be up to three minor version older than the API server, so 1.32 of API server.
If it is running, then the cube proxy can be 1.32, which is the same 1.3, one, 30 and 29, which
are the three older versions, then the cube API server.
The next important part is related to the controller manager scheduler and the Cloud controller manager.
So one important point here is that these components must not be newer than the cube API server instances
that they communicate with.
In an ideal scenario, they are expected to match the cube API server minor version, but may be up
to one minor version older to allow live upgrades.
For example, if API service 1.32, then the scheduler controller manager and the Cloud Controller Manager
that are supported is either 1.32 and 1.31.
Now here it is important to note that one minor version older is supported to allow live upgrades.
Why?
Let's say that your API server is 1.32 and all other components are also 1.32.
Now tomorrow you want to upgrade your Kubernetes cluster and you are upgrading the cube API server.
So what you will do, you will upgrade the cube API server from 1.32 to 1.33.
Now at this stage, kube API server is running at 1.33, while all other components are running at 1.32.
So you want to ensure that the live upgrades do not create issues.
And this is the reason why this part of compatibility is made available.
And the last part is related to kubectl.
Ideally, kubectl is supported within one minor version of the kube API server.
So if kube API server is 1.32, the kubectl supported is 1.33, 32, and 31.
Now note that one minor version it can be older or newer.
Over here.
Along with that, if you want to read about the version skew policy in detail, there is a specific
documentation related to it where they have explained all of this in more detail.
So when you are upgrading your Kubernetes cluster, it is very important that you are aware about the
latest version skew policy before you start with the upgrade process.
Great.
So that's a quick overview.
And with this we'll conclude today's video.
